8f53073c2a577f9d: CAIRO: Egyptian authorities released independent journalist Lina Attalah from custody on Tuesday, hours after she was detained and a court ordered her website shut, her lawyer told AFP.
Attalah is one of Egypt's most prominent journalists, and her detention had sparked swift condemnation from rights groups and press freedom advocates.

A court had earlier fined Attalah three million Egyptian pounds (around US$53,400) for operating website Mada Masr without a licence, the maximum possible penalty for the misdemeanour she was charged with, and ordered the website's closure.
"Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine," her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari said, referring to a three million Egyptian pound (US$53,400) fine.
"In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds," he told AFP.
Attalah's defence team has appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing is scheduled for Nov 11, Azhari said.
News of the release followed condemnation by rights groups of the detention, which they described as a sharp escalation in Cairo's crackdown on press freedom.
Mada Masr says it has not received a response from authorities about its licence application since 2023.
The hours-long detention comes weeks after the arrest of an entire fact-checking newsroom on charges of fake news, which are frequently levelled against media seen as critical of the government.
Hossam Bahgat, head of prominent rights group the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), was present at the court and gave AFP an account of events leading up to the arrest.
During Tuesday's hearing, the defence team said the judge ordered the room cleared except for Attalah and her lawyers, before security officers also entered the room.
Attalah's eight-person defence team had made procedural requests that were denied by the court, which then announced it had appointed its own lawyer for the journalist.

"In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," Bahgat said.
"Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes."
"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer – who had not uttered a single word – and entered them into the official record," he added.
The judge then announced the fine and ordered Mada Masr's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before security personnel in the room detained Attalah.
'Wiping out' free press
This was the sixth case brought against Attalah and Mada Masr in as many years, but none had ever gone to trial.
Egypt is currently holding 26 journalists in connection with their work, according to an EIPR tally.

The crackdown "can only mean that Egypt's security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely", Bahgat had told AFP when Attalah was referred to trial.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF) branded the court's decision "outrageous" and "shameful", urging authorities to release Attalah "at once".
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict.
"If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe," CPJ regional director Sara Qudah said in a statement.
Earlier this month, six journalists from fact-checking platform Matsadaash were charged with terrorism offences after being arrested in a series of raids in September.
EIPR, which represents the journalists, said they had reported torture following their arrests, allegations denied by the interior ministry.
Authorities accused them of links to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and spreading "rumours and false news" to undermine confidence in state institutions and incite people to protest.
They are currently being held in pretrial detention, which rights groups say can be extended for months or years before detainees are released or face trial.

3a3134792b629381: MUMBAI: An Indian court has allowed Bollywood actor Imran Khan to remain in the country until at least Nov 2, local media reported on Tuesday, suspending a government order requiring him to leave for allegedly breaching immigration laws by participating in a protest.
Khan, 43, is a US citizen and was asked to leave the country by Oct 28 after he was accused of joining protests in Mumbai against the country's election chief this month.
Under Indian law, the participation of foreigners in political protests can be treated as a violation of immigration and visa rules.
Khan appealed against the order in the Bombay High Court, saying it was unconstitutional and arbitrary, local media reported.
There was no evidence to show that Khan had participated in the protest and mobilised a crowd, his lawyer said in the appeal, legal website Live Law reported.
On Tuesday, the Bombay High Court postponed the hearing to Nov 2 for technical reasons and said the order Khan had challenged would remain on hold until then, legal website Bar and Bench posted on X.
There has been no official statement from Mumbai Police on Khan's case. The city's police chief did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
A nephew of actor Aamir Khan, Imran belongs to a prominent film family. He acted in several hit Bollywood films from 2008 to 2015 before suddenly retiring.

His partner, Lekha Washington, said in a post on her Instagram page on Oct 12 that she, Khan, his mother and a cousin had walked towards the protest site to ask about a friend who had been detained by police and were immediately surrounded by media representatives.
"He (Imran) responded to the questions of the media, saying we have no demands, we are not part of an organisation," Washington said in the post.
Both Khan and Washington posted pictures from inside what appeared to be a police van on the day of the protests, smiling into the camera.

The rally in Mumbai was one of several protests across the country demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over what opposition parties and activists say is a revision of voter lists that benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party.

523acbb87abcb447: BHUBANESWAR: A severe cyclone began making landfall in India's Andhra Pradesh state in the early hours of Wednesday, bringing high-speed winds and heavy rain that uprooted trees and disrupted power supplies, authorities said.
Thousands of people were evacuated along India's eastern coast this week, and some train and flight services were cancelled ahead of Cyclone Arnab's arrival.
The India Meteorological Department said wind speeds over the landfall area were forecast to reach 125-135km/h, with gusts of up to 150kph, over the next four hours before decreasing gradually.
A storm surge of 1.5 to 2.5 metres above the normal tide was very likely to inundate low-lying areas of Andhra Pradesh over the next six hours, the IMD said.
No loss of life had been reported so far, although trees had been uprooted in several places and power supplies disrupted, the office of Andhra Pradesh's chief minister said.
Arnab is sweeping in from the Bay of Bengal, a major region for tropical cyclones that has spawned deadly storms along India's east coast.
A super cyclone that killed nearly 10,000 people when it hit Odisha in October 1999 remains one of the country's deadliest natural disasters.

Beyond health and financial protection, AIA PUBLIC Takaful embodies the spirit of Berkat Sama-Sama, demonstrating how takaful can create value not only for individuals and families, but also for the wider community.

Through the eligible family takaful plan to which A-Plus Health360-i is attached, participants may choose to donate their eligible surplus to the AIA Penyala Harapan Charity Fund, which supports charitable organisations and community initiatives.
This allows participants to safeguard their health and financial wellbeing while contributing to initiatives that benefit people in need and create a positive impact on society.
As healthcare needs continue to evolve, A-Plus Health360-i represents a new generation of medical takaful solutions that combine protection, wellness and purpose.
Designed to support participants through different stages of life, the rider reflects AIA PUBLIC Takaful's commitment to helping people live Healthier, Longer, Better Lives.

2ca718826c712381: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — Parliament is expected to scrutinise government decisions, debate laws and examine how public money is spent, but who manages the institution itself?

That question is at the heart of the Parliamentary Service Act 2025, which came into force on October 1, restoring a dedicated service intended to give Parliament greater control over its staffing, finances and administration after more than three decades under the government’s administrative structure.

The law establishes the Parliamentary Service Council to oversee the service, with the aim of strengthening Parliament’s institutional independence from the executive, which refers to the prime minister, Cabinet and government ministries.
The council came into focus on October 14, when the Dewan Rakyat approved four MPs, two from the government and two from the Opposition, to sit on it.
But what does the council actually do, who sits on it, and how far does its authority extend? Malay Mail explains.
What is the Parliamentary Service Council?
The Parliamentary Service Council is the body responsible for matters relating to the Parliamentary Service, a separate service established under the Parliamentary Service Act 2025 (Act 869).

In practical terms, it is intended to give Parliament greater say over the staff and resources needed to carry out its work, rather than leaving these matters largely dependent on administrative arrangements within the executive.
The council does not replace Parliament or take over MPs’ responsibility for debating legislation and scrutinising the government.
Instead, it oversees the administrative machinery that supports those duties.
Who sits on the council?
The council will have 16 members drawn from Parliament and the public service.
The President of the Dewan Negara serves as chairman, while the Speaker of the Dewan Rakyat is co-chairman.
The other parliamentary members are the Deputy President of the Dewan Negara, two Deputy Speakers of the Dewan Rakyat, two senators and four MPs.
The four MPs must comprise two government representatives and two Opposition representatives.
They are nominated by the Dewan Rakyat’s Committee of Selection and approved through a resolution of the House.

The Dewan Rakyat on October 14 approved Ramkarpal Singh (Pakatan Harapan-Bukit Gelugor) and Datuk Seri Hasni Mohammad (Barisan Nasional-Simpang Renggam) as the government’s representatives, with Datuk Seri Dr Ronald Kiandee (Perikatan Nasional-Beluran) and Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan (PN-Kota Bharu) representing the Opposition.
The two senators are similarly nominated by the Dewan Negara’s Committee of Selection and approved by a resolution of the Senate.
Dewan Negara president Datuk Seri Awang Bemee Awang Ali Basah has said the two senators will be appointed once the Dewan Negara convenes from November 30.
Dewan Rakyat Speaker Tan Sri Johari Abdul has said the council is expected to be formed by December.
The council also includes the clerk to the Dewan Negara and the clerk to the Dewan Rakyat.
Its three ex-officio members are the Treasury secretary-general or a representative, the director-general of Public Service or a representative, and Parliament’s chief administrator.
Ex-officio members do not have voting rights.
That leaves 13 voting members, of whom two are Opposition MPs.
This composition brings together parliamentary leaders, government and Opposition representatives, and officials from the Treasury, the Public Service Department and Parliament’s administration.
What does the council actually do?
The Act gives the council four broad responsibilities.
First, it appoints members of the Parliamentary Service and determines their terms and conditions of appointment, subject to the applicable legal framework.
Second, it oversees financial matters relating to the service.
Third, it develops and implements training and development programmes for Parliamentary Service staff.
Fourth, it may take other steps reasonably necessary to administer the service and carry out its functions.
These responsibilities matter because Parliament needs professional staff to support its proceedings, maintain official records, assist committees and handle legislative and administrative work.
The council may also establish committees to help carry out its responsibilities.
Does the council run Parliament day to day?
Not directly, as the Act hands that job to Parliament’s chief administrator.
The chief administrator is responsible for the institution’s overall administration and management, including its day-to-day affairs and the financial matters of the Parliamentary Service.
The chief administrator acts under the council’s general authority and directions, and is also the council’s secretary.
This creates a division of responsibility: the council oversees the service and provides general direction, while the chief administrator handles its administration and daily operations.
The Act also provides for separate committees dealing with staff promotions, disciplinary matters and appeals.
How will the council make decisions?
The council must meet as often as necessary to carry out its functions.
At least seven members are required for a quorum.
Members other than ex-officio members are entitled to vote, and decisions are made by a majority of those present and voting.
If the votes are tied, the chairman has a casting vote.
The Act also requires members to disclose any direct or indirect interest in a matter being considered.
A member with such an interest cannot take part in the relevant deliberations or decision.
These provisions establish formal procedures for decision-making and help guard against conflicts of interest.
How will it make Parliament more independent?
The central idea is to give Parliament greater control over its own administrative needs, rather than relying on arrangements managed through the executive branch.

When the Parliamentary Service Bill was before Parliament in 2025, Law and Institutional Reform Minister Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said said the service was intended to strengthen Parliament’s institutional independence and support the separation of powers between the legislative, executive and judicial branches.
She also highlighted the need for professional support for MPs, including help with drafting legislation and access to research expertise for both government and Opposition lawmakers.
Such support could help MPs and parliamentary committees examine bills, assess government policies and scrutinise public spending more effectively.
However, the council itself does not hold the government politically accountable.
Its role is to manage the administrative support that Parliament needs to perform its oversight functions, while MPs and parliamentary committees remain responsible for carrying out that scrutiny.
Will Parliament control its own budget?
Not entirely, because the Act leaves it to the government to provide the funds.
Section 12 of the Act provides that the government must supply sufficient funds annually for the Parliamentary Service to enable the council to perform its functions.
The council is responsible for overseeing financial matters relating to the service, but the statutory provision does not itself spell out every step in the budget-submission process.
Azalina said that the intended arrangement would allow Parliament to submit budget proposals directly to the Finance Ministry without first obtaining approval from the Prime Minister’s Department.

That distinction matters: the obligation to provide sufficient funding is set out in the law, while the direct-submission procedure is part of the minister’s explanation of how the arrangement is intended to work.
Does this mean Parliament is completely separate from the civil service?
No, as the Act keeps links between the Parliamentary Service and the wider public administration.
The Act establishes the Parliamentary Service as a service separate from the general public service.
For example, Section 11 requires the Chief Administrator to be appointed from among members of the federal general public service.
The arrangement therefore gives Parliament a distinct administrative structure under the law without severing all connections with the wider public service and government financial systems.
What does this mean for accountability?
The council creates a formal structure for managing Parliament’s staff, finances and administrative resources, with rules governing appointments, training, voting and conflicts of interest.
Azalina has argued that stronger institutional support would help MPs serve as the “eyes and ears of the people”, including by enabling them to identify wastage and hold the government accountable.
But a new administrative structure alone cannot guarantee more effective scrutiny.
That will also depend on whether MPs make effective use of the support available to them, how parliamentary committees conduct their work and how well the council fulfils its responsibilities.

Ultimately, the council’s significance lies in helping Parliament manage the resources it needs to do its job, while leaving the responsibility for questioning the government and holding it accountable with MPs and parliamentary committees.
2719214bd09deb76: WASHINGTON, Oct 28 — Americans vote on November 3 in midterm elections that will decide whether President Donald Trump’s Republicans retain control of Congress or spend the final two years of his term confronting Democratic majorities.
High living costs, the war with Iran and Trump’s poor approval ratings have helped Democrats expand the electoral map, with unusually tight contests even in Republican strongholds.
But polling errors, redrawn districts and record campaign spending make the outcome uncertain.
The arithmetic

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the upper chamber of Congress, as a 50-50 tie would leave Republicans in charge through Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are contested. It is currently made up of 218 Republicans and one Republican-aligned independent, 214 Democrats, and two vacancies.
Democrats need at least 218 seats in the lower chamber to clinch a majority in the new session.
Senate: eight battlegrounds

North Carolina: The state’s Democratic ex-governor Roy Cooper faces Republican operative Michael Whatley in a bid to flip the seat being vacated by retiring Senator Thom Tillis, a vocal Republican Trump critic. Strong polling for Cooper has prompted both parties to shift some spending elsewhere, but the contest remains key for Democrats.

Texas: Democrat James Talarico, a Christian progressive, faces Trump-backed state Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose controversies have helped turn a longtime Republican stronghold into a closely watched contest. Paxton retains a loyal conservative following and enormous outside financial support.

Ohio: Former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown seeks a comeback against Republican Jon Husted, who was appointed to replace Vance when he became vice president. Among the country’s most expensive races, it’s also a test of whether economic discontent can shift a state that has moved sharply rightward.
Maine: Republican Susan Collins faces former state Senate leader Troy Jackson. She has repeatedly survived difficult elections in a state that votes Democratic for president.
Alaska: Former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola challenges Republican Daniel Sullivan. Her strong standing among voters has made another Trump-voting state unexpectedly competitive.
Iowa: Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek compete for retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst’s seat, while soaring agricultural and energy costs are prominent issues.

Kansas: Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton is challenging Republican Roger Marshall in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. Tight polling has prompted Trump to campaign for Marshall.
Michigan: An important Republican pickup opportunity pits former congressman Mike Rogers against progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
House: watch the suburbs
New York’s 17th district: Republican Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in a Hudson Valley seat won by Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.
Nebraska’s 2nd: Republican Don Bacon’s retirement leaves a competitive Omaha-area seat contested by Republican Brinker Harding and Democrat Denise Powell.

Pennsylvania: Republican incumbents Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan and Scott Perry face closely watched Democratic challenges. Nearby New Jersey’s 7th district, where Rebecca Bennett challenges Republican Tom Kean Jr, is also in play.
Virginia’s 2nd: Democrat Elaine Luria seeks to reclaim the coastal seat she lost to Republican Jennifer Kiggans in 2022.
Iowa: Three Republican-held districts in the state’s east and center could provide an early indication of whether Democrats are making broad gains.
Signs of a wave?

For an indication of the scale of any Democratic advance, watch two Republican-held House districts in Virginia: the 1st, where Shannon Taylor challenges Robert Wittman, and the 5th, where former congressman Tom Perriello wants to unseat John McGuire.

A Democratic gain in Kentucky’s Republican-leaning 6th district, or unexpected defeats for Republicans in Florida’s 13th and Wisconsin’s 1st, would likewise signal a particularly broad electoral swing.

Conversely, Democrats face dangers of their own in redrawn districts, including Alabama’s 2nd, where Shomari Figures is defending his seat, and Texas’s 34th, where Vicente Gonzalez faces Republican Eric Flores. — AFP
215dfd8a559b3278: PORT DICKSON, Oct 28 — Designed like a traditional Malay village house with a classic touch, Warong Nora in Kampung Permatang Pasir, Linggi, here, offers more than just traditional Negeri Sembilan cuisine, inviting visitors to step back in time and experience the charm of rural life in days gone by.

Located about 40 kilometres from Seremban, the family-run eatery is adorned with various antiques that seem to transport visitors to a bygone era. However, beyond the old furniture and household items decorating the premises, one attraction stands out — a collection of vintage telephones spanning different eras, shapes and designs.

From home telephones that once connected families and friends to public payphones that have become increasingly rare, each item has its own story to tell, earning Warong Nora a reputation among visitors as a ‘mini telephone museum’.

Among the most eye-catching exhibits is a public telephone more than 70 years old, which not only sparks curiosity but also serves as a popular backdrop for visitors to take photographs and record videos.

The unique collection reflects the deep interest of its owner, Hamdzan Ali, 69, who began collecting old telephones in the 1990s. Over the years, his hobby grew into a personal collection that not only filled his home in Taman Tuanku Jaafar, Senawang, but also became a distinctive feature of Warong Nora.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Hamdzan Ali with his son-in-law, Safuan Mohd Pikri. Hamdzan established the eatery as a space to share his passion for antiques with the public. — Bernama pic
Hamdzan said some visitors had dubbed the eatery a mini telephone museum because, among the many antiques on display, were telephones of various types, including mobile phones.
“Many visitors are attracted to the designs of the telephones here, some dating back to the 1960s to the 1980s, in addition to the food we serve.

“They say our eatery is different from the cafes and restaurants with antique decorations they have visited before. Since I used to work at Telekom Malaysia, it was not too difficult for me to obtain old telephones that were no longer in use,” he told Bernama.

Hamdzan said his collection comprised telephones of various types and designs, including those once used in homes and public payphones, which were an essential facility in people’s daily lives in the past.

When met by Bernama at Warong Nora recently, the father of six said his passion for collecting antiques stemmed from a longing for the old household items at his family home in Seliau, Rantau, which was destroyed after his elder brother set fire to it while clearing the house.

The TM retiree travelled to various parts of the state in search of old treasures, building a personal collection estimated to number nearly 1,000 items, with total expenditure amounting to hundreds of thousands of ringgit.

All the items are carefully stored and maintained at his home. However, when almost every corner of the house had been filled with antiques, the idea emerged to open Warong Nora on a plot of land belonging to his wife, Che Tom Md Dom, 66, in Linggi.
Together with his son-in-law, Safuan Mohd Pikri, 40, and his second child, Norashimah Hamdzan, Hamdzan established the eatery as a space to share his passion for antiques with the public.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Smoked baung fish cooked in ‘masak lemak cili api’, a signature Negeri Sembilan dish, is among the main attractions at Warong Nora. — Bernama pic
At the same time, the family introduced traditional Negeri Sembilan cuisine, with smoked baung fish cooked in masak lemak cili api — a rich, spicy coconut milk gravy — among its signature dishes.
Prepared by Norashimah and her mother, Che Tom, the generations-old recipe is cooked only upon receiving customers’ orders to preserve the freshness and authentic flavour of the dish.

Safuan said although customers sometimes had to wait longer for their meals, particularly during peak hours, this had not deterred regular patrons from returning to enjoy dishes prepared personally by his wife and mother-in-law.

“People who visit Linggi will certainly look for smoked baung fish cooked in masak lemak cili api. What makes Warong Nora special is that we use wild baung fish caught from rivers rather than farmed fish.
“We continue to preserve Linggi’s traditional cooking methods, using fresh turmeric, bird’s eye chillies and fresh coconut milk.

“What makes Linggi’s smoked fish masak lemak cili api special is the use of Vietnamese coriander leaves, which enhance its aroma, and calamansi lime, which adds a tangy flavour. Some districts use bilimbi, but we opt for calamansi lime to preserve our traditional taste,” he said, adding that the eatery also offered other traditional village dishes.
Safuan said Warong Nora, which began operations three years ago, continued to enjoy encouraging patronage despite opening only three days a week — Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

“We are not focused on profit. What matters to us is allowing visitors to experience the authentic taste of Linggi’s traditional cuisine, particularly smoked baung fish in masak lemak cili api, as well as other traditional Negeri Sembilan dishes.
“Besides that, our eatery also offers a place for customers to relive fond memories of village life and their mothers’ home cooking,” he said. — Bernama
8308eef20daa5dcd: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — The Fire and Rescue Department (JBPM) is strengthening its operational and logistical capabilities through asset modernisation efforts and the exploration of new technologies, including Unmanned Remote Systems (URS) involving two Fire Fighting Robots (FFRs).

JBPM director-general Datuk Seri Nor Hisham Mohammad said the move was crucial for ensuring the department remained prepared to deal with various emergencies, including fires, accidents, rescue operations and large-scale disasters.

He said the replacement of vehicles and equipment would be carried out in stages based on the age and operational capability of existing assets, including the acquisition of 80 Fire Rescue Tenders (FRTs).
According to him, JBPM acquired 686 FRT units between 2001 and 2026, while the requirement based on operational norm stood at 592 units.

“Based on these figures, 372 of the 592 existing units (63 per cent) have exceeded 10 years of service. As such, the procurement of 80 replacement FRT units and 150 existing CFRT (Compact Fire Rescue Tender) units is expected to have a tangible impact on the department’s preparedness and operational capabilities and service delivery in the coming years,” he told Bernama.

Besides replacing vehicles, Nor Hisham said the department was also focusing on improving response times, especially in areas that had yet to meet the stipulated targets, through the construction of new fire stations and the continuation of ongoing projects.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Rescue personnel participate in a disaster response exercise as part of preparations for the North-east Monsoon season. — Bernama pic

“In a bid to modernise our operational capabilities, the department also plans to acquire URS equipment involving two FFR units, in line with technological advancements to support firefighting and rescue operations.

“The provision of personal protective equipment (PPE), particularly firefighting protective clothing, as well as the addition and replacement of basic rescue equipment, are also important requirements to ensure the safety of personnel while on duty,” he added.

Nor Hisham said the department was also focusing on utility vehicles, logistics for its K9 Unit and operational facilities to support personnel mobility, especially during search and rescue operations and disaster management.

In terms of personnel welfare, the JBPM is focusing on the construction and maintenance of quarters, with total project costs amounting to RM241.6 million, including a ceiling allocation of RM35.1 million for 2027.

A total of RM16 million has also been allocated for facility maintenance, in addition to the approval of redevelopment and modernisation of ageing fire stations, namely the Fire and Rescue Stations (BBP) in Perai, Jalan Perak, Jerantut, Muar and Sarikei.
Nor Hisham expects efforts to strengthen assets, facilities and personnel capabilities to improve asset reliability, departmental preparedness and emergency response capabilities.

In the long term, JBPM is open to exploring the use of electric vehicles (EVs) for FRTs and utility vehicles, with assessments to be conducted on operational suitability, travel distances, battery capacity, charging infrastructure, technical requirements and the total lifecycle cost of the assets.

To support these efforts, the government has approved a Development Expenditure (DE) allocation of RM1.8 billion for JBPM under Budget 2027 to carry out 96 ongoing and new projects, comprising physical development, infrastructure and the procurement of vehicles and equipment, with a ceiling allocation of RM200 million for the year.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A Fire and Rescue Department helicopter is deployed during a search and rescue operation in Bidor, Perak. — Bernama pic
“This allocation is extremely important, particularly in meeting the need to replace FRTs, provide protective clothing and other firefighting and rescue equipment,” he added.

On Saturday (Oct 24), Minister of Housing and Local Government Nga Kor Ming announced the allocation of RM200 million under Budget 2027 to enhance firefighters’ efficiency in carrying out rescue missions and preparedness for fire-related disasters. — Bernama
95f4a464beea2fc0: ALOR SETAR, Oct 28 — Ice cream made from buffalo milk not only offers something different, but is also said to be far more nutritious than regular commercial ice cream.

Buffalo milk ice cream entrepreneur Mohamed Zamberi Abdul Razak said the uniqueness of the ice cream lies in its higher natural protein content, while the fat structure in the animal’s milk also has a significant impact on the final product.
“Most ice creams on the market rely on added stabilisers to achieve a smooth texture and sweetness, but this buffalo milk ice cream takes advantage of the milk’s own physical properties.

“Because of its high protein content, the resulting soft-serve ice cream has a very soft, fluffy and dense texture. When blended with ice cream powder, the high protein content gives the ice cream a creamier taste,” he told Bernama here.
Mohamed Zamberi, who sells the ice cream under the “Karabao” brand near Pekan Rabu here, claimed that buffalo milk is more nutritious than ordinary cow’s milk.

“Many people are afraid to try buffalo milk because they are concerned about its strong or distinctive smell and taste often associated with the animal. However, the vanilla and chocolate-flavoured ice cream products we produce have no unpleasant smell or taste.

“Here, we sell vanilla, chocolate and mixed-flavour ice cream in containers for RM4.90. Besides ice cream, customers can also try buffalo milk yoghurt and drinks such as coffee, tea and Milo mixed with buffalo milk,” he said.
Mohamed Zamberi said one litre each of vanilla- and chocolate-flavoured ice cream is produced every day, with around 40 to 50 containers of ice cream prepared for customers.
He said he sources Murrah buffalo milk from several suppliers, including those in Pendang, Perak and Selangor, and supplies have so far remained sufficient.

“Not many people have dared to explore this product because the risks are quite high, including the fact that buffalo milk is very sensitive to temperature and can spoil easily if not handled carefully,” said Mohamed Zamberi, who was involved in a buffalo project in Langkawi in 2008 and 2009. — Bernama
acd9154ed738c734: From Moaz Nair
According to an opposition lawmaker, the government providing subsidies is like “giving fish to the people”. Eventually, they say, the people will become lazy.

Critics frequently echo this sentiment, arguing that giving cash aid and relief to lower- and middle-income groups acts as a drag on national output. They view it as a pure consumption cost that fails to enhance economic productivity.
However, empirical macroeconomic data suggests this perspective is deeply flawed.
Far from being simple welfare relief, targeted cash transfers — such as Malaysia’s Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) — serve as vital mechanisms for strategic economic investment.
When structured effectively, cash assistance significantly amplifies both immediate aggregate demand and long-term labour productivity.

To make the full transition into a high-income nation, our fiscal discourse must evaluate how cash assistance behaves when scaled to the middle 40% (M40) income group. We need to shift the paradigm from merely maintaining a socio-economic floor to actively constructing an upward economic ladder.
The B40 multiplier effect
To understand the productivity debate, one must first isolate the short-term stimulus created by lower-income households, which is driven by a high marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
Because B40 families operate near subsistence levels, they immediately re-inject almost every additional ringgit received into the economy for basic necessities.
This capital flows directly into local micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) whose owners, in turn, pay suppliers and workers.
Studies reviewed by the World Bank demonstrate that cash transfers consistently yield a high economic multiplier, where every RM1 distributed generates upwards of RM2 to RM2.50 in local GDP growth.
Beyond immediate retail velocity, mitigating extreme financial stress unlocks long-term labour output by alleviating cognitive load and physical deprivation.
Cash aid provides the financial breathing room necessary for individuals to undergo technical and vocational education and training (TVET) or make the transition towards higher-value employment.
Furthermore, when paired with healthcare initiatives like PeKa B40 (ProtectHealth B40), cash transfers improve nutritional status and preventive care, fostering a healthier, more alert workforce.

This intervention yields its greatest dividends in future human capital, as targeted aid is reinvested into children’s education, mitigating school dropout rates and systematically elevating the skills ceiling of the next generation.
Not a policy panacea
Nevertheless, economists caution that cash handouts alone do not constitute a policy panacea.
While cash aid triggers rapid market circulation, it can induce minor, localised demand-pull inflation if supply chains face structural constraints.
It also carries a latent risk of welfare dependency if the programme lacks clear exit policies.
Financially, the model relies heavily on state revenue, requiring meticulous fiscal balancing despite indirectly bolstering tax revenues through increased economic activity.

Ultimately, cash aid only drives lasting productivity if it is structurally integrated with broader reforms, such as wage restructuring, digital transformation for small businesses, and proactive job placement programmes.
Upward social mobility for the M40
The economic dynamics shift fundamentally when evaluating the potential of expanding cash assistance or fiscal relief to the M40 income group.
Funding the M40 results in a lower immediate economic multiplier but yields a significantly higher long-term return on high-value productivity.
While B40 interventions focus primarily on survival, aid targeted at the M40 drives upward social mobility and formal structural investment.

Because their baseline survival needs are secured, M40 households exhibit a lower MPC and direct surplus funds towards professional education upgrades, debt reduction, healthcare insurance, and domestic tourism.
While this slower velocity of money tempers the immediate multiplier effect, it channels institutional capital into formal consumer sectors that employ a vast segment of the domestic workforce.
As the backbone of the nation’s skilled workforce, reducing cost-of-living pressures on the M40 unlocks high-value labour productivity through two primary channels:

Professional upskilling: M40 individuals are highly likely to utilise financial relief or tax-rebate equivalents to fund professional certifications or postgraduate diplomas. This creates a talent pool capable of anchoring high-value foreign direct investment (FDI).

Mitigating burnout: It eases the intense economic pressures faced by the “squeezed middle” — a demographic often ineligible for heavy subsidies yet highly vulnerable to inflation — thereby stabilising white-collar productivity.
Furthermore, unlike the B40, a portion of the disposable income left with the M40 enters the broader financial ecosystem as productive capital.
These individuals channel surplus funds into unit trusts, voluntary Employees Provident Fund (EPF) contributions, or retail equities, deepening national investment liquidity.
This liquidity also enables M40 professionals to seed side hustles, micro-digital enterprises, and freelance consulting ventures, fostering broader innovation across the digital economy.
Conclusion
Ultimately, the core differences between funding these two socio-economic tiers lie in their macroeconomic outcomes.

While the B40 target impact drives immediate retail consumption, rapid market velocity, and basic labour survival through direct cash transfers, the M40 target impact enables discretionary spending, high-value professional upskilling, and managerial efficiency through delivery mechanisms like tax reliefs, education credits, and housing incentives.
Maximising Malaysia’s economic potential requires a balanced, dual-track approach rather than an adversarial policy debate.
Funding the B40 establishes the vital economic and social floor, ensuring the baseline labour force remains stable, healthy, and participant in the economy.

Conversely, providing targeted relief to the M40 builds the economic ladder, offering the upward momentum necessary to push the workforce out of the middle-income trap and into high-productivity industries.
True economic foresight lies in managing both ends of this continuum simultaneously.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
bc50494740a113e0: Menurut seorang Ahli Parlimen pembangkang: “Kerajaan bagi subsidi, ibarat bagi ikan kepada rakyat. Lama-lama rakyat jadi malas." Golongan pengkritik juga kerap mengulang sentimen ini dengan berhujah pemberian bantuan tunai dan kelepasan fiskal kepada kumpulan pendapatan rendah dan pertengahan hanya menjadi beban kepada output negara. Mereka melihatnya semata-mata sebagai kos penggunaan yang gagal meningkatkan produktiviti ekonomi.

Bagaimanapun, data makroekonomi empirikal menunjukkan perspektif sedemikian amat tersasar. Jauh daripada sekadar bantuan kebajikan biasa, pemindahan tunai bersasar—seperti Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) di Malaysia—bertindak sebagai mekanisme penting bagi pelaburan ekonomi yang strategik. Apabila distrukturkan dengan berkesan, bantuan tunai mampu merangsang kedua-dua permintaan agregat jangka pendek dan produktiviti tenaga kerja jangka panjang secara signifikan.

Untuk beralih sepenuhnya menjadi sebuah negara berpendapatan tinggi, wacana fiskal kita mesti menilai bagaimana kesan bantuan tunai ini apabila diperluaskan kepada kumpulan pendapatan pertengahan 40% (M40). Kita perlu mengubah paradigma daripada sekadar mengekalkan lantai sosioekonomi kepada usaha membina tangga mobiliti ekonomi ke atas.
Kesan pengganda golongan B40

Bagi memahami perdebatan mengenai produktiviti ini, seseorang itu perlu melihat terlebih dahulu kesan rangsangan jangka pendek yang dicetuskan oleh isi rumah berpendapatan rendah, yang dipacu oleh kecenderungan mengguna sut (MPC) yang tinggi. Memandangkan keluarga B40 hidup pada tahap kais pagi makan pagi, mereka akan menyuntik semula hampir setiap ringgit tambahan yang diterima ke dalam ekonomi serta-merta untuk keperluan asas.

Modal ini mengalir terus ke dalam perusahaan mikro, kecil dan sederhana (PMKS) tempatan, di mana pemiliknya pula akan membayar pembekal dan pekerja. Kajian yang disemak oleh Bank Dunia menunjukkan pemindahan tunai secara konsisten menghasilkan kesan pengganda ekonomi yang tinggi, di mana setiap RM1 yang diagihkan mampu menjana pertumbuhan KDNK tempatan sehingga RM2 hingga RM2.50.

Selain merancakkan aktiviti peruncitan segera, usaha mengurangkan tekanan kewangan yang melampau juga secara aktif membuka potensi output tenaga kerja jangka panjang dengan meringankan beban kognitif dan kekurangan fizikal. Bantuan tunai memberikan ruang bernafas dari segi kewangan yang membolehkan individu mengikuti pendidikan dan latihan teknikal dan vokasional (TVET) atau beralih ke sektor pekerjaan yang bernilai lebih tinggi.

Tambahan pula, apabila digabungkan dengan inisiatif kesihatan seperti PeKa B40, pemindahan tunai dapat meningkatkan status pemakanan dan penjagaan kesihatan pencegahan, sekali gus membentuk tenaga kerja yang lebih sihat dan cergas. Intervensi ini memberikan pulangan terbesar terhadap modal insan masa hadapan, memandangkan sebahagian besar bantuan bersasar dilaburkan semula untuk pendidikan anak-anak, mengurangkan kadar keciciran sekolah, dan mengangkat tahap kemahiran generasi pekerja akan datang secara sistematik.
Bukan penawar mutlak segala dasar

Bagaimanapun, ahli ekonomi mengingatkan pemberian tunai sahaja bukanlah penawar mutlak untuk semua dasar. Walaupun bantuan tunai mencetuskan pusingan modal pasaran yang pantas, ia boleh mendorong inflasi tarikan permintaan setempat yang kecil sekiranya rantaian bekalan menghadapi kekangan struktur. Ia juga membawa risiko kebergantungan kepada kebajikan sekiranya program tersebut tidak mempunyai dasar keluar (exit policy) yang jelas.

Dari sudut kewangan, model ini amat bergantung kepada hasil negara, yang memerlukan pengurusan fiskal yang teliti meskipun ia menyumbang kepada peningkatan kutipan cukai secara tidak langsung melalui aktiviti ekonomi yang rancak. Akhir sekali, bantuan tunai hanya akan memacu produktiviti yang berkekalan jika ia disepadukan secara struktural dengan reformasi yang lebih luas, seperti penyusunan semula gaji, transformasi digital untuk perniagaan kecil, dan program penempatan pekerjaan yang proaktif.
Mobiliti sosial ke atas bagi M40

Dinamik ekonomi berubah secara asas apabila kita menilai potensi memperluaskan bantuan tunai atau kelepasan fiskal kepada kumpulan pendapatan M40. Menyalurkan dana kepada M40 menghasilkan kesan pengganda ekonomi jangka pendek yang lebih rendah, namun memberikan pulangan jangka panjang yang jauh lebih tinggi terhadap produktiviti bernilai tinggi. Jika intervensi B40 tertumpu terutamanya kepada kelangsungan hidup, bantuan yang disasarkan kepada M40 pula memacu mobiliti sosial ke atas dan pelaburan struktural formal.

Disebabkan keperluan asas mereka telah dipenuhi, isi rumah M40 menunjukkan kadar MPC yang lebih rendah dan mengalihkan lebihan dana ke arah peningkatan pendidikan profesional, pengurangan hutang, insurans kesihatan, dan pelancongan domestik. Walaupun kitaran wang yang lebih perlahan ini mengurangkan kesan pengganda segera, ia menyalurkan modal institusi ke dalam sektor pengguna formal yang menggaji sebahagian besar tenaga kerja domestik.
Sebagai tulang belakang kepada tenaga kerja mahir negara, langkah mengurangkan tekanan kos sara hidup terhadap M40 dapat melonjakkan produktiviti buruh bernilai tinggi melalui dua saluran utama:

Peningkatan kemahiran profesional: Individu M40 berkemungkinan besar akan menggunakan pelepasan kewangan atau nilai setara rebat cukai untuk membiayai pensijilan profesional atau diploma pascasiswazah. Ini melahirkan kumpulan bakat yang mampu menarik pelaburan langsung asing (FDI) bernilai tinggi.

Mengurangkan keletihan melampau (burnout): Langkah ini meringankan tekanan ekonomi sengit yang dihadapi oleh golongan "pertengahan yang tersepit"—demografi yang sering tidak layak menerima subsidi besar tetapi amat terdedah kepada inflasi—sekali gus menstabilkan produktiviti pekerja kolar putih.

Selain itu, berbeza dengan B40, sebahagian daripada pendapatan boleh guna yang berbaki pada golongan M40 akan memasuki ekosistem kewangan yang lebih luas sebagai modal produktif. Individu-individu ini menyalurkan lebihan dana ke dalam amanah saham, caruman sukarela Kumpulan Wang Simpanan Pekerja (KWSP), atau ekuiti runcit, yang memperdalam kecairan pelaburan nasional. Kecairan ini juga membolehkan golongan profesional M40 memulakan perniagaan sampingan, perusahaan digital mikro, dan usaha perundingan bebas, yang memupuk inovasi lebih luas dalam ekonomi digital.
Kesimpulan

Kesimpulannya, perbezaan teras antara pembiayaan kedua-dua lapisan sosioekonomi ini terletak pada hasil makroekonomi mereka. Impak sasaran B40 memacu penggunaan runcit segera, pusingan pasaran yang pantas, dan kelangsungan tenaga kerja asas melalui pemindahan tunai langsung. Sebaliknya, impak sasaran M40 membolehkan perbelanjaan budi bicara, peningkatan kemahiran profesional bernilai tinggi, dan kecekapan pengurusan melalui mekanisme penyampaian seperti pelepasan cukai, kredit pendidikan, dan insentif perumahan.

Memaksimumkan potensi ekonomi Malaysia memerlukan pendekatan dwi-trek yang seimbang, bukannya perdebatan dasar yang bersifat bertentangan. Membiayai B40 menyediakan lantai ekonomi dan sosial yang penting bagi memastikan tenaga kerja asas kekal stabil, sihat, dan terlibat dalam ekonomi.

Sebaliknya, menyediakan pelepasan bersasar kepada M40 membina tangga ekonomi, menawarkan momentum ke atas yang diperlukan untuk melonjakkan tenaga kerja keluar daripada perangkap pendapatan pertengahan ke arah industri berproduktiviti tinggi. Pandangan jauh ekonomi yang sebenar terletak pada keupayaan mengurus kedua-dua hujung spektrum ini secara serentak.
Penulis ialah pembaca FMT.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
3255255e23732e20: PETALING JAYA: A few taps on your phone can now open the door to investing, whether you are buying cryptocurrency or letting a robo-advisor manage a portfolio.

Digital tools can offer convenience, lower costs and allow people to start investing with smaller amounts. Yet, as access becomes easier, licensed financial planner Bryan Zeng reminds investors to take time to understand the risks.
“Having access to something easily does not mean it is safe,” Zeng told FMT Lifestyle.
For those exploring these platforms, Zeng suggests asking:
“Do I understand what I am buying?”
“Who makes the investment decisions?”
“Who holds my assets?”

The answers help investors understand what their money is invested in, who decides what is bought or sold and whether their investment records can be verified directly with the institution holding their assets.

“A salesperson may give you a statement to say that you have this amount of money in these investments. But can you go to the company behind this salesperson and obtain the same statement that shows the same amount?” asked Zeng, a member of the Financial Planning Association of Malaysia.
Alongside understanding the investment, Zeng said it is important to check who is offering it.
Investors can verify whether the company and representative are authorised through the Securities Commission Malaysia’s (SC) Investment Checker.
Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) lists licensed banks and insurers, while the Federation of Investment Managers Malaysia maintains a register of unit trust and private retirement scheme consultants.
Zeng also recommends checking the SC’s and BNM’s alert lists, as well as the Royal Malaysia Police’s Semak Mule portal for bank accounts linked to reported scams.
But these checks are only a starting point: the absence of a warning does not guarantee that an offer is genuine.
Business registration alone is no reassurance either, Zeng cautioned.
“Being incorporated with the Companies Commission of Malaysia only means that the business is registered. It does not mean that they are authorised to provide financial services,” explained Zeng, 48.
Even finding a company on an authorised list is only part of the check: scammers may use its name to promote a fictitious scheme.

Zeng, who is the CEO of FA Advisory, has seen his own firm impersonated this way. He recalled one particularly painful case: a retiree who contacted the firm lost almost his entire retirement fund to the scam.

To protect yourself, Zeng advised contacting the company using a number you find independently to verify the representative and offer. He also urged investors to confirm where their money goes - a request to transfer funds to an individual’s account is a red flag.
How scammers build trust
Beyond impersonating legitimate firms, scammers may use deepfake videos of prominent personalities to make investment offers appear credible, Zeng said.
Once people show interest, scammers often move conversations into WhatsApp or Telegram groups, where accomplices pose as successful investors, sharing fabricated returns and photographs of cash.
A salesperson then contacts the potential victim privately, promising extraordinary returns.
Then comes the countdown: invest now or miss out. “They don’t give you time to verify their claim. That is their strategy,” said Zeng.
Fake apps make the scam look convincing by displaying growing balances. Victims are encouraged to invest more but once a large sum is deposited, Zeng added, withdrawals are blocked.
When victims become suspicious and question this, scammers may cut off access to the app and become uncontactable.
Even seeking help can expose victims to another scam.

Zeng recalled advising a victim who found an advertisement offering legal help to recover his losses. At Zeng’s suggestion, he called the law firm directly and discovered that someone was impersonating a genuine lawyer who offered no such service.
If you suspect a scam, act immediately:
Contact your bank’s fraud hotline to report any transfers and stop further transactions.
Call the National Scam Response Centre at 997.
Alert the SC if investments are involved.

“Making a police report with all the details you have is very important,” he emphasised. These include transfer receipts, recipient account details, advertisements, chat histories and contact information.
Investing may take only a few taps, but checking where your money is going deserves more time. An offer that pressures you to skip those checks is one you can afford to miss.
For financial guidance, watch the Financial Planning Association of Malaysia’s weekly ‘Money Mastery’ videos on Facebook or explore your spending habits through its Money Style Check quiz.
d0058f9358c0b939: BERLIN: Marcel Sabitzer scored deep into stoppage time as Borussia Dortmund fought off Werder Bremen 3-2 in the second round of the German Cup on Tuesday.

With the hosts two goals up thanks to goals from Serhou Guirassy and Carney Chukwuemeka, former Dortmund striker Niclas Fuellkrug came off the bench and scored twice in four minutes to level the scores.

With the match headed for extra-time, the one-time Bayern Munich and Manchester United midfielder Sabitzer curled a superb free kick into the top left corner to see Dortmund through to the next round.
"I'm really happy it went in. My right foot has always been pretty decent. It's good for the team, but also good for me," Sabitzer told Sky Germany.

On a season-long loan from West Ham, Fuellkrug has now scored in his past seven Bremen games and has 11 goals in nine matches this season, having scored just three times in 18 months at the London stadium.
Earlier on Tuesday, Christoph Baumgartner scored twice in the final 12 minutes to rescue a 10-man RB Leipzig in a 2-1 win at third-division Rot-Weiss Essen.
Essen's Lucas Brumme gave the hosts the lead after nine minutes and Leipzig's task got harder just before half-time when Nicolas Seiwald picked up a second yellow card.
Leipzig, who won the competition back-to-back in 2022 and 2023, were on track for an early elimination until Baumgartner scored two goals inside five minutes.
The night before the match, Essen fans had concreted over the away fan entrance, with city authorities in a race against time to clear the entrance before kick-off.
Robin Koch, Jonathan Burkardt and Younes Ebnoutalib scored as Eintracht Frankfurt cruised to a 3-1 win at three-time winners Hamburg.
Germany starlet Said El Mala scored a brace as hosts Cologne eliminated Union Berlin 5-0.
Elsewhere, Bundesliga sides Mainz and Elversberg also bit the dust, losing to Bochum and Darmstadt respectively, while Augsburg and Borussia Moenchengladbach won to reach the last 16.
On Wednesday, holders Bayern host Magdeburg in Harry Kane's first match since winning the Ballon d'Or on Monday.
9c864f502d6d8dc0: CORPUS CHRISTI: US secretary of state Marco Rubio made a rare appearance Tuesday alongside president Donald Trump on the midterms campaign trail, visiting an oil tanker filled with Venezuelan crude just days before the crucial vote.
Rubio and vice president JD Vance are widely viewed as top contenders to carry the Republican Party into its post-Trump era in the 2028 election.
But while Vance has been crisscrossing the country in recent weeks to rally support ahead of the Nov 3 polls, it is very unusual for the top US diplomat to engage in such domestic political trips.
On Tuesday, Trump called Rubio on stage at his campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, remarking: "He's so popular."
"We love Marco," he added, beckoning Rubio to join him at the podium as the crowd chanted Rubio's name.
A state department official said Rubio was travelling with Trump in his capacity as National Security Advisor. He is the first person to hold both key foreign policy jobs since Henry Kissinger.

"He needs time with the president on all kinds of issues. The president will be on the go, so being on the plane with him gives (Rubio) a chance to talk to him about these items," the US official added on condition of anonymity.

While the official did not elaborate on the nature of these issues, their comments come against the backdrop of wars in the Middle East and Ukraine - as well as elections in Israel and the upcoming vote in the United States.
Rubio, who made a run for president in the 2016 election, has yet to say if he would throw his hat in the ring again in 2028.
Trump remains a dominant figure in the Republican party, and the 80-year-old has yet to endorse a successor.
Until now, Rubio, the first Hispanic and first fluent Spanish speaker to be the top US diplomat, has steered clear of the campaign trail.
He has instead focused on a series of international trips - including visits to Uzbekistan and India last week.
He is also set to host a meeting of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta, Georgia, on Friday and Saturday.
Venezuelan oil

Trump and Rubio's showcasing of an oil tanker carrying one million barrels of Venezuelan crude comes as affordability remains a top worry for American households grappling with steeper costs of gasoline and other goods.
The oil, Trump said, is set to be processed at Texas refineries.
Relations between Washington and Caracas have warmed after the United States toppled longtime leader Nicolas Maduro in a military operation in January.
Maduro's vice president Delcy Rodriguez took power after his ouster, and has been complying with Trump's demands for Caracas to open its energy industry to American companies.
Trump is hoping this showcase of supply from Venezuela will bolster support from voters, vowing that gasoline and diesel costs will soon cool.
Global oil prices have surged since US-Israel strikes targeting Iran in late February triggered Tehran's retaliation in blocking off a key route of energy transit, the Strait of Hormuz.
This has translated into higher costs at the gasoline pump and sparked a surge in transportation fees for businesses, threatening further spillover into consumer prices.
Republicans are wary that voter anger over inflation, stoked by Trump's launch of war on Iran, could trigger a "blue wave" of Democrats winning in the midterms.
The US leader has since been working to rally loyal supporters who often stay home when he is not on the ballot, as Republicans push to retain control of both chambers of Congress.

1df80ae8316d8b8c: PARIS: Stan Wawrinka bid farewell to tennis as he brought the curtain down on a decorated 24-year career following a first-round exit at the Basel Open on Tuesday.

The 41-year-old Swiss announced earlier in the season that his last tournament as a professional would be the ATP 500-level event in his home country, and a 7-5, 7-6 (7/2) defeat by Czech Jiri Lehecka brought an end to the career of the three-time major champion.
Former world number three Wawrinka, along with Andy Murray, was the only player to win multiple Grand Slams in a period dominated by Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic.
He bested Nadal to win his first Grand Slam at the Australian Open in 2014, before beating Djokovic in the French Open final the following season and then again in the US Open title match in 2016.
Alongside his compatriot Federer, the Lausanne native won the Davis Cup for Switzerland and claimed gold in the doubles at the 2008 Beijing Olympics.
On court in Basel, Wawrinka's every point won, as well as several trademark booming one-handed backhands, was greeted by wild cheers from the partisan home crowd.
But Lehecka got his nose in front with a break of serve in the 11th game and sealed the opening set with an ace as he held to love.
A tight second set rumbled towards a tie-break, but it was just a step too far for Wawrinka as his 21st-ranked opponent took firm control to seal the breaker and the match.
Wawrinka, who enjoyed a farewell ceremony in Basel on Monday, did a circuit of the court to thank the supporters before disappearing down the tunnel off-court for the last time.
"He won the biggest tournaments, so for me to be here in his moment is a little bit weird," Lehecka told Sky Sports.
"But at the same time, it's a pleasure, and I will never forget this match."
However, fans will have one more chance to see the Swiss in action this year.
Wawrinka announced in June that he will throw a farewell party on Dec 19 in Geneva with Federer and Murray also on the card of the "One last backhand" event.
Elsewhere, second-seed Arthur Fils beat his fellow Frenchman Giovanni Mpetshi Perricard 7-6 (7/5), 7-5 to reach the round of 16.

Spanish third seed Rafael Jodar cruised past Chilean Alejandro Tabilo in straight sets, while top seed Ben Shelton battled past his American compatriot Aleksandar Kovacevic 6-7 (4/7), 7-6 (7/3), 7-6 (7/4).
Djokovic, who trained with his old friend and foe Wawrinka ahead of the tournament on Sunday, will open his campaign on Wednesday against Ugo Humbert of France.
5a622a2de58e506e: JERUSALEM: Israel's wartime election appeared deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, a potential setback for veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if the projections hold. Neither side had a clear path to power, but rival Gadi Eisenkot's larger bloc could give him the first chance to form a government.
The stalemate could yet work in Netanyahu's favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
Turnout was 77.7 per cent, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around seven percentage points higher than in the previous election in 2022.
Israel's three major networks updated their exit polls, giving Eisenkot's bloc a two-seat edge over Netanyahu's Likud-led camp, at 52-50.

The remaining 18 seats were allocated to unaligned Arab parties in the exit polls. But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to a majority despite his bloc's lead.
Some Israeli media outlets, including pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, projected a far stronger showing for Netanyahu and his parties, saying they would collectively win 60 seats.

Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties as potential kingmakers. No single party has ever won 61 seats outright in the 120-seat Knesset, making coalitions the norm.
It was the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Anti-Netanyahu boost
While there was no clear outcome, the exit polls reflected the strength of the anti-Netanyahu opposition.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: "Don't let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home."

Eisenkot, 66, a hawkish former military chief who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu's strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist on domestic issues.
He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticising the prime minister's leadership.

Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hardline approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
Eisenkot says Israel's response — a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities — was a failure because Hamas remains in charge.

"Dear Democrats, a decision was made," Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party and a Netanyahu rival, said at a party rally after polls closed. "The nation has given us a sacred duty: to translate the trust they have placed in us into action, to fortify democracy, to save Israel and to provide true defence for the state."

The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, erupted in whistles and applause when exit polls were released at the close of voting, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

"We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here," said Faten Gattas, a Joint List candidate, in a speech at the alliance's headquarters in Nazareth. Candidates hoped that high Arab voter participation would allow them to play a decisive role in preventing Netanyahu's coalition — the most far-right in Israel's history — from returning to power.
A record turnout

Long lines had formed outside polling stations as voters turned out in huge numbers, grappling with the trauma of Israel's deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon's Hizbollah and Iran that followed.
While Netanyahu was criticised for the country's biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by assassinating top leaders of Hamas, Hizbollah and Iran.

The policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises.
His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back.
He entered the election facing longstanding corruption charges, which he denies, and criticism over intelligence failures that allowed Hamas-led fighters to carry out their attack.
Netanyahu campaigned on an endorsement from US President Donald Trump, his ally in the war against Iran.

97b25bec90c6866e: BRASILIA: Defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil and is travelling to the United States despite a court order banning him from exiting the country, US media reported Tuesday.
The son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro lost elections to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday and refused to concede defeat.

The right-wing senator on Monday said a Supreme Court justice had ordered him to hand over his passports. Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose his parliamentary immunity.
The 45-year-old was heading to Florida, CNN reported Tuesday, citing an anonymous official source. Other US media confirmed he was heading to the country.
The US state department said Tuesday that it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, without confirming his travel plans.
A police source told AFP that the senator's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been cancelled, adding that "there is no formal record of Flavio Bolsonaro leaving the country."
But he has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP.
Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho expressed shock over reports that the defeated candidate had fled Brazil.
"We still don't have any news about his whereabouts," he told reporters in Brasilia on Tuesday.
"I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it," Marinho said.
"That was the only communication we had."
Scare tactic
Flavio Bolsonaro said Monday that the ban on his exit from Brazil amounted to a scare tactic.
"I never had any intention of leaving the country. I will surrender my passports and defend myself against this travesty," he said in the video posted on Instagram.
US president Donald Trump, a close ally of Jair Bolsonaro, on Monday said Brazil's elections were "rigged" following the defeat of Bolsonaro junior.
Flavio's brother Eduardo, a US-based former lawmaker, maintains close ties with the White House.
Last week, he told a US podcast that Flavio Bolsonaro should leave Brazil in the event of electoral defeat, given the active probes into his activities.
In his Monday statement, Lula's challenger also said he would lead the opposition to the leftist government.

Following Lula's victory with 51.8% of the vote, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting.
Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro over bad weather in parts of the country.
In his father's footsteps
All bets were on a Bolsonaro win after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month.
He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later.
Separately on Tuesday, the Supreme Court ordered police to investigate alleged foreign funding of Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign and other interference from abroad such as social media "manipulation."
Lula's campaign complained about interference in the election by Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, claiming "algorithmic manipulation."
Meta denies taking any actions to favor one side in the election, but previously said that some of Lula's campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.

7880953207904af3: FLEETWOOD: Arsenal suffered one of the most humiliating defeats in their history as the Premier League champions were stunned by fourth-tier minnows Fleetwood in a League Cup penalty shoot-out on Tuesday.
Mikel Arteta's side crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible fourth round upset after the tie finished 1-1 in normal time.
Arsenal's Bruno Guimaraes had his penalty saved by Jay Lynch in the shoot-out, and Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood's winner.
Aaron Loupalo-Bi's first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalised after the interval.
Arsenal's 16-year-old rising star Max Dowman was sent off for violent conduct in the closing stages.
Arteta paid the price for prioritising Sunday's Premier League trip to Liverpool as his decision to make nine changes backfired spectacularly.
No one would have predicted Arsenal's embarrassment regardless of Arteta's selection gamble.
They had moved level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City after a 2-0 victory over Everton on Saturday.
But instead of extending their run of 11 wins from their 13 previous games, Arsenal returned to north London red-faced after a loss that ranks among the darkest days in the club's glittering history.
Arsene Wenger's Arsenal suffered a shock League Cup loss against fourth-tier Bradford on penalties in 2012.
Arteta's team were beaten by second tier Southampton in the FA Cup last season and also lost to Nottingham Forest, then in the Championship, in the same competition in 2022.
Supporters of an older vintage will recall Arsenal's 1969 League Cup final loss against third-tier Swindon and their 1992 FA Cup exit at fourth-tier Wrexham.
But even those painful defeats cannot compare to this remarkable result.
For once, Arsenal fans will not have fond memories of Highbury – Fleetwood's ground shares the same name as the Gunners' ancestral home before their move to the Emirates Stadium in 2006.

Fleetwood's tiny 5,327-capacity ground – where goals are celebrated with a burst of children' cartoon song Captain Pugwash over the tannoy – it is a far cry from the famous marble halls and dignified grandeur of Arsenal's former stadium.
Now it will be remembered forever as the site of Arsenal's most chastening loss in the Arteta era.
Fleetwood boss Matt Lawlor wept tears of joy as disbelieving fans flooded the pitch to celebrate their club's astonishing victory.
'Cod Army' uprising
Only Myles Lewis-Skelly and Viktor Gyokeres kept their places from the Everton game, with teenagers Dowman and Marli Salmon starting, while 18-year-old winger Ceadach O'Neill made his debut.
Languishing in 18th place in League Two, Fleetwood had lost their previous two league games against Exeter and Cheltenham, yet they showed no signs of being intimidated by their illustrious visitors.
After an eight-minute delay due to an unauthorised drone flying over the stadium, Arsenal were caught cold on a windy night by the Irish Sea.
Fleetwood are nicknamed the 'Cod Army' in reference to the town's fishing industry, so it was somewhat fitting that a mistake from Salmon netted their opener in the 21st minute.
Salmon's lack of experience was brutally exposed when Loupalo-Bi muscled his way past the 17-year-old with ease, racing into the penalty area to plant a low finish past debutant keeper Illan Meslier.
Arsenal monopolised possession after that shock, but Arteta grew visibly agitated with their lack of cutting edge.
Arteta sent on Martin Odegaard at half-time, and Gyokeres bagged Arsenal's equaliser five minutes later.
It was a scrappy effort that left Fleetwood feeling aggrieved as Gyokeres wrestled with his marker before poking O'Neill's ball past Lynch from close range.
Dowman saw red in the 85th minute, dismissing for kicking out at Harrison Neal after a strong challenge from the Fleetwood midfielder.
Although it looked a harsh decision, Arteta was unimpressed with Dowman, giving him a stern word as the midfielder trudged off.
Both teams scored their first three penalties in the shoot-out, but Guimaraes was denied by Lynch, and Haughey held his nerve to seal the biggest shock in League Cup history.

0f39ea2acf21946d: The Malaysian legal system, largely inherited from the British adversarial model, offers a legal framework that stands in stark contrast to the inquisitorial approach favoured by major religions.
The difference lies in philosophy. Inquisitorial traditions are designed to seek fairness, truth, and community responsibility, while adversarial systems tend to prioritise procedure and advocacy.
This is one of the chief causes of the massive case backlogs plaguing our courts.

Malaysia is not alone. Across the Commonwealth, chief justices and judiciaries have yet to recognise the wisdom of moving away from adversarial and aristocratic procedures inherited from their former colonial masters. These outdated practices remain the primary culprits behind endless delays.

By contrast, the Panchayat system in India—a council of village elders employing inquisitorial methods—delivers fair and immediate justice. I have personally witnessed this in my ancestral village of Thopputhurai, Vedaranyam, Tamil Nadu.
That experience later became the foundation for my University‑cum‑Court Annexed Arbitration (UCCA) model, designed to clear case backlogs.

Litigants and the public want immediate solutions to their disputes and hope for instant decisions. Instead, they are subjected to the opposite: a long, convoluted process culminating in lengthy, wordy judgments issued by the trial and appellate courts.

From my observation as both lawyer and judge, the adversarial system has little to do with genuine justice or fairness. Instead, it rewards those who can present their version of the truth most convincingly.
Quite often, being “economical” with the truth can secure a win. In most cases, it becomes a contest of who can craft the more compelling narrative.
In such a scenario, an advocate’s role is to construct a persuasive narrative based on selective facts to sway the judge. Whether the narrative reflects truth or reality is secondary.

More often than not, trial judges are not subject‑matter experts and simply act as arbiters of competing narratives. On the other hand, when a trial judge is an expert in the field, truth and falsehood in both evidence and submissions can be quickly discerned.
The tragedy is that our system rarely prioritises such expertise. Instead, the Commonwealth suffers from backlogs generated by courtroom rhetoric—often pursued for financial gain.

The British aristocratic litigation procedure imposes no strict timeframe on the legal fraternity or judiciary, leaving justice perpetually delayed. Consequently, the legal maxim “justice delayed is justice denied” has become the defining failure of Commonwealth courts, a shameful hallmark of their dysfunction.

The UCCA model offers a way forward. By appointing subject‑matter experts of unquestionable integrity—chosen by disputing parties after a conflict arises—false rhetoric can be dismantled and backlogs eliminated. Such a system would restore credibility to the process and return justice to being timely, fair and accessible.

Through the mercy of the Almighty, the UCCA path may witness the return of the legal profession’s soul, reminding lawyers and judges alike that their calling is not to perpetuate delay or profit from complexity, but to uphold justice as a sacred trust.
In this way, the profession can recover its moral compass, aligning itself once more with the values of major religions that emphasise truth, compassion and accountability.

I trust that my three previously published articles"Is the British litigation system a failure?", "Justice not a privilege, costs not a weapon" and "Academia can rescue democracy’s spoilt child" —will together offer a definitive pathway to addressing the challenges faced across the Commonwealth, helping to restore public faith in the judiciary while saving governments billions of dollars.

Timely justice is not merely a procedural expectation, it is an unwritten constitutional right. The legal industry and the judiciary are strictly obliged to uphold it. When they fail, they risk being seen by the lay public as scammers, not guardians of justice.

I have studied this crisis for over two decades. My firm conclusion is that the legal industry and judiciary have failed in their constitutional duty to deliver timely justice, eroding public trust and undermining the very legitimacy of the courts.

Chief Justices across the Commonwealth would serve the public well by coming together to confront the backlog crisis and work toward resolution. Such gatherings must go beyond rhetoric and commit to structural reform.
The UCCA model offers them the opportunity to revamp their court systems. It can help dismantle the culture of delay, restore faith in the judiciary, and reaffirm the profession’s higher calling.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

5c819a565532267f: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country's occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely — or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions.

In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread.
