5f7fa0d561693f82: From Sameer Khan
When I was growing up, almost every boy dreamed of becoming a policeman. It was a simple dream, born out of the games we played and the heroes we imagined ourselves to be.

In households, the older brother would be the first to wear the badge of authority, with a pair of toy handcuffs ready to complete the uniform. He would arrest the villain, usually one of his younger siblings, and the living room would become a police station.

But if you happened to be the only male child, only one person was worthy of the criminal role – your father. With all seriousness as a child, we will place those handcuffs around our father's wrists. He would play along, surrendering himself to the authority of a little boy who, only moments earlier, could barely tie his own shoelaces.
Looking back, it was never about catching a criminal. It was about feeling brave and heroic. For a while, we were the good guys, protecting a world that existed in our imagination.

Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency director-general Shuhaily Zain, now facing charges involving junior police officers, deserves neither condemnation before trial nor unquestioning defence because of his rank. The law must be allowed to establish the facts.
What matters is that the process remains fair with evidence speaking louder than speculation and public confidence is protected.

In the end, an institution's strength lies not in protecting its own, but in ensuring that justice is served without fear or favour. However, there is also another court that sits every day, without a judge, without lawyers and without the need to wait for evidence to be tested.

It is the court of public opinion. Its verdicts can be swift, unforgiving and difficult to reverse. In an age when every allegation finds its way onto our screens, reputations can be damaged long before the courts have had their say.
Yet, when public confidence in an institution is already under strain, even one more controversy can reopen old wounds.
The question is no longer simply whether an individual is guilty, but whether the institution itself has done enough to earn the public's trust.
The numbers deserve our attention and so I did a little research.

Figures presented in Parliament show that criminal cases involving police personnel rose from 378 in 2023 to 407 in 2024 and 463 in 2025. Deaths in police custody increased from 12 to 13 and then 22 over the same period.
Meanwhile, rights group Suara Rakyat Malaysia documented more than 190 instances of police misconduct in 2024, with half of the cases receiving no action beyond investigation.
These figures do not establish guilt in any individual case, but they do explain why human rights groups continue to demand greater transparency.

When the public repeatedly hears questions raised about those entrusted to uphold the law, silence and pause can no longer be the response. Institutions must answer not merely with assurances, but with evidence that accountability is real.

KLIA is not merely a gateway to Malaysia. It is a strategic point in a global battle against drug trafficking. The sharp rise in drug cases and seizures reported in 2026 should concern every Malaysian.

International syndicates do not care about our reputation and our laws as well as the lives they destroy. They look for weaknesses and exploit them. This is precisely why enforcement must be firm and intelligence must be effective, with every allegation of wrongdoing investigated thoroughly and if any found guilty, they must be handled tactfully.
At stake is not simply the security of our borders, but the credibility of the institutions entrusted to protect them.
As children, there was something special about the idea of upholding the law, catching the bad guy and standing on the side of what was right.

As adults, we place that same hope in those entrusted with protecting our nation, particularly those guarding our borders. We expect them to rise above personal differences and serve a greater purpose.
Of course, the truth must be established by evidence, not assumption. But the questions deserve to be asked.
Perhaps the real question is not who wears and holds the badge and rank, or who stands accused. It is whether we have built an institution where truth can stand on its own, without fear or favour.

For in the end, a uniform may command respect, and rank may demand obedience, but neither can command the truth. And when the dust settles, we must ask ourselves one simple question: Are we teaching the next generation to uphold the law, or merely to learn how to use it against one another?
Sameer Khan is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

8a823511a2d42568: SEATTLE: Boeing posted a bigger third-quarter loss than expected on Tuesday, as supply-chain challenges and production delays in its commercial airplane division overshadowed stronger margins across the rest of the company.

Shares of the US planemaker fell 2.5% in premarket trading even as Boeing continues to recover from years of crises and controversies that dented its reputation, drained cash and saddled it with a heavy debt load.

During the quarter, Boeing secured certification for the 737 MAX 7 from US regulators, won the US Navy's sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter contract and generated free cash flow for another quarter, while certification of the larger MAX 10 followed in October.

The company attributed the performance to less profitable jetliner deliveries and higher production costs, including from its supply chain.

Boeing has struggled to increase 737 output from 42 jets a month to 47, which it hoped to hit during the summer. It has not been able to make wings fast enough, CEO Kelly Ortberg said at an industrial conference in September.

8e8f0387002bfcb3: The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple's first foldable phone. Despite the company's big talk about its "precision-engineered" hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device's impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use.

The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin.

Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo's screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself.

b5463b29c1314232: Three-quarters of corporate board members expect AI to deliver productivity gains and cut costs, yet only three percent of organizations have hit their targets, according to researchers at Gartner.
The figures came out of the analyst’s HR Symposium, where it also reported that 38 percent of companies are over budget on AI spending, and 85 percent still plan to spend even more next year.

"Ultimately, organizations will not generate cost savings from AI at this point," said CV Viverito, senior director analyst for Gartner's HR practice. "The greater opportunity is to use AI to do things that weren't possible before, such as shifting employee time into new capabilities, outcomes, and sources of growth."

Gartner claims that at least 75 percent of biz leaders are out of step with the broader organization on where AI creates value, which stalls transformation efforts and muddies how to position the workforce and bag those returns.

Organizations should concentrate AI on the work that matters most to the business, with HR helping execs to agree on the top bets based on strategy, Gartner advises. Companies should also spread existing AI expertise across the business rather than wait to hire scarce specialists, and give managers room to redesign the work around the technology, it adds.
Only about one in five employees' time is freed-up by AI, letting them redirect toward more innovative work, the HR Symposium heard.

“There isn’t a struggle to create capacity, that’s happening already as organizations redesign work,” claimed Viverito. “What organizations are struggling with is how to make that capacity usable and redirecting it to what is valuable.”
That starts - or so we're told - by giving employees the skills to take on higher-value, AI-enabled work, which, of course, means spending more on training.

The takeaway is that getting a return on AI projects is harder than expected, and companies are going to have to stick with it and be prepared to institute changes in the way they and their staff work before they see any tangible benefits.

A recent Forrester report concluded that AI will likely account for 20 percent of all business technology spend next year, yet more than half of CIOs are likely to miss their ROI targets for the technology

Another piece of research from KPMG earlier this year found that most UK business leaders aim to keep AI at the top of their spending priorities even if it isn’t working, with 65 percent planning to maintain investment whether they see immediate measurable returns or not.

How long that resolve lasts is an open question. Private equity giant Apollo Global Management is the latest to raise doubts, noting this week that the "Magnificent Seven" tech giants are reaping the rewards of all that AI spending, while the rest of the S&P 500 has seen no sign of AI boosting productivity growth. ®

57f9e735d3ff4182: Dating back to around 400 CE and made of dichroic glass, the Lycurgus Cup is notable for exhibiting different colors depending on the light. (It gets its name from the scene depicted on its surface, of King Lycurgus of Thrace.) Light it from the front, and the cup looks green; light it from behind, and the color changes to a deep red. University of Sheffield scientists have re-created the original recipe to produce a contemporary glass sculpture with the same optical effect.

The cup is considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world, one of just 40 glass cage cups that survived. Exactly why the unusual color effects of the Lycurgus Cup occurred was a mystery until 2007, when a team of scientists discovered the color shifts were due to the presence of nanoparticles in the glass—the result of Roman artisans adding finely ground gold and silver into the mix. Those nanoparticles change how the electrons in the cup vibrate in response to light so that the color one sees shifts with the observer’s vantage point.

As we reported in 2019, it’s a similar phenomenon to the one responsible for the shifting colors of 19th-century daguerreotypes due to the scattering properties of nanoparticles. The Romans added salt when they melted the silicon (sand) to make the glass, and those salts contained gold atoms. In the melting process, those atoms aggregate and produce nanoparticles, which in turn produce the colors. It’s how any stained glass is made. It's also similar to how the precise lattice-like structure of photonic crystals produces iridescent colors in nature, like the wings of butterflies, or opals.

Apple is far from the only foldable maker to stumble over production creases in its foldable phone hardware. Samsung's Galaxy Fold was delayed in 2019 after reports of dust creeping under the screen and borked displays, prompting swift design tweaks.

Francisco Jeronimo, veep of Worldwide Devices at IDC, said: "The early reports of inner display failures on the iPhone Duo show that even a company with Apple's engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables."

Jermonimo noted Apple had not yet shared any figures or the scale of the problems. "Some of the images circulating online are recycled or altered, so caution is needed before drawing conclusions about the whole production run."

However, Samsung's "fast and transparent response" limited damage to the category, he added, and how Apple, "handles this first-generation issue will shape buyer confidence in the category well beyond its own sales."
Apple's statement to The Register indicates taking the problem seriously, and it will be eager to avoid a repeat of the iPhone 4, which was marred by the infamous "you're holding it wrong" furor.
With the iPhone Duo, the last thing Apple wants is to be accused of telling customers "you're folding it wrong." ®
d151abbfa32e2a37: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 27 — While China remains Malaysia’s largest source of international students, the Education Malaysia Global Services (EMGS) said applications from other countries are growing.

EMGS chairman Datuk Ahmad Shalimin Ahmad Shaffie said China accounted for approximately 41 per cent of applications in 2023, but the proportion has since declined as Malaysia attracts students from more markets.
“By 2025, East Asia as a whole, including China, accounted for less than 37 per cent. In the first four months of 2026, China’s share stood at approximately 27 per cent.
“Alongside continued growth in total applications, these figures indicate an increasingly important contribution from other markets,” he said in a statement.
Ahmad Shalimin said regional figures further reflected this growing diversity.

“In 2025, applications from South Asia and Central Asia each grew by 41 per cent, while South-east Asia recorded 28 per cent growth, Africa by 20 per cent and the Middle East and North Africa by 19 per cent.
“Over the past decade, EMGS has received applications from 189 countries,” he added.
He said this was why the question raised by Gareth Liu Zi Yuan in his article, “More international students, but from where?”, published in Malay Mail on October 22, deserved attention.
“We welcome the discussion on broadening Malaysia’s international student community and ensuring that those who come here receive a rewarding education and experience.
“Malaysia is ranked 14th globally as an international education destination, welcoming students from nearly 180 countries. That reach provides a strong foundation,” he said.

However, Ahmad Shalimin said Malaysia must now strengthen existing connections, develop opportunities in underrepresented markets and ensure international students have good reasons to recommend the country after graduation.
He said EMGS conducts marketing activities across seven regions, with more than 50 programmes worldwide each year.
“Education fairs, forums, international exhibitions, school visits and counsellor engagements connect Malaysian institutions with students, families and education partners across different markets.
“Recent efforts have included Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Kenya, Türkiye and Central Asia, alongside participation in the European Association for International Education exhibition in Glasgow,” he said.
Ahmad Shalimin said engagement with neighbouring ASEAN countries, particularly Indonesia, and nearby regions such as South Asia remained a priority.
“These efforts also include creating more accessible pathways for students through mobility programmes and scholarship opportunities.

“By strengthening established partnerships while developing opportunities in emerging markets, Malaysia can broaden its international student community and build lasting education connections,” he said.
He added that student mobility programmes were also strengthening Malaysia’s ties with Europe.

“The number of mobility students from France increased from 827 in 2025 to 939 in 2026, a rise of 13.5 per cent, reflecting continued interest in Malaysia for short-term international study experiences,” he said.
Ahmad Shalimin said Malaysia’s international education presence was also expanding through local universities operating overseas.
“UCSI University’s campus in Dhaka, established in 2023, became Bangladesh’s first approved foreign university branch campus.
“It brings Malaysian education closer to students in their home country while strengthening the international presence of our institutions,” he said.
He said these developments reflected the growing international recognition of Malaysia’s higher education sector.
“Universiti Malaya is ranked 56th in the QS World University Rankings 2027 and joint 194th in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2027.

“Sunway University’s position as 11th globally for International Outlook in the latter rankings further illustrates the international engagement of Malaysia’s public and private institutions,” he said.

“For prospective students, these achievements help make Malaysia’s educational strengths visible. For our institutions, they reinforce the importance of sustained academic quality and international cooperation,” he added.

On student pass applications, Ahmad Shalimin said EMGS facilitates digital submissions, document verification, academic screening and application tracking, while the Immigration Department of Malaysia remains the approving authority.

“EMGS’s published processing charter is 14 working days for complete applications. Alya, our AI-powered assistant, also answers queries around the clock, helping students navigate visa requirements and application procedures.

“Upon arrival, the International Student Arrival Centres (ISAC) at KLIA Terminals 1 and 2 provide round-the-clock assistance before immigration clearance, including guidance on access to dedicated lanes.
“This dedicated support helps students navigate their first experience in Malaysia with greater confidence,” he said.
He also said EMGS offered internship opportunities to international students, having welcomed interns from Iran, Myanmar, Indonesia, Turkmenistan and several African countries.
“These placements provide opportunities to apply knowledge, develop professional skills and experience a Malaysian workplace.
“Support from higher education institutions is equally vital through career guidance, industry partnerships and internship opportunities that prepare students for their future careers,” he said.
Ahmad Shalimin said internationalisation also benefited Malaysian students studying alongside their international counterparts.
“Shared classrooms, research and community activities expose students to different perspectives and help them build international networks within their own campuses.
“As Malaysian universities become better known abroad, employers and academic partners become more familiar with their qualifications and expertise.
“The relationships developed through education can support future research, institutional cooperation and professional opportunities,” he said.
He added that international graduates also helped strengthen Malaysia’s global connections.

“Their experiences influence what families, colleagues and future students understand about Malaysia. They become informal ambassadors whose achievements and personal stories give our higher education sector a human face,” he said.
Ahmad Shalimin said studying in Malaysia should offer international students more than just an academic qualification.
“Learning alongside people from different backgrounds, participating in community life and navigating new experiences can nurture empathy, resilience and a stronger sense of responsibility.

“Our ambition is for students to leave with the knowledge to pursue their careers and the character to contribute meaningfully to society, carrying a lasting connection with Malaysia wherever life takes them,” he said.
b7e18dcc23157f49: <!--kg-card-end: html--> In Sunday’s edition of the New York Times, Marissa Mayer, former president and CEO of Yahoo, told her interviewer something so absurd it’s since gone viral.

Struggling with the “impossible task” of naming three things that she loves about her own 10 year old daughter, the New York Times reports, Mayer asked the AI assistant she just launched to do that thinking for her. It delivered the perfect answer, Mayer said: “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover.” Everyone is piling onto that absurd anecdote right now, rightfully so. What she has to say about gender in tech, however, is more out of touch than that.

Saying sensational things on the record — especially knowing that the reporter will not be able to resist using such a shocking story as the lede — is a savvy strategy. For someone as influential as Mayer, telling the list story is transparently a result of years of media training. Mayer is selling her new app, Dazzle, which accesses your camera roll and analyzes your life based on the photos you take. It’s disturbing to see her talk about relinquishing basic cognitive skills like “plan a birthday party” to AI. But the rest of the story gets into something Mayer has talked about for more than a decade: “the gender card,” as she’s called it.

“I never play the gender card,” she told Steven Levy in a 2015 interview. “The moment you play into that, it’s an issue. [...] In technology we live at a rare, fast-moving pace. There are probably industries where gender is more of an issue, but our industry is not one where I think that’s relevant.” She repeats similar sentiments in Sunday’s NYT interview.

The height of Mayer’s career coincided with the girlbossification of everything, during the Lean In era, when Notorious RBG and “well behaved women rarely make history” mugs were everywhere. She’s been asked about gender in tech one million times, and has mostly dismissed it. But a decade after the tech girlboss reigned, her thoughts on this haven’t seemed to evolve much.

Later in the NYT piece, she brushed off the notion that gender has any bearing on who gets to participate in the tech industry. She also brushes off a question about bias baked into AI models, something that’s been studied and proven extensively, and instead names female AI executives like Fei-Fei Li as the reason well-documented bias doesn’t exist. She asserts that passion overrides gender, as if just being “passionate” enough erases decades of women’s experiences in the tech workforce.
“To me, gender fades into the background. I talk about passion as a gender neutralizing force,” she told the NYT. “If you’re excited about something, gender doesn’t matter.”

Meanwhile, male figureheads of the AI industry are out here posting slop videos about sperm on main. Half of women in tech leave the industry by 35, earn 84 cents to their male counterparts’ dollar, and women founders receive half the amount of funding that male founders do.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> Earlier this month, event organizers canceled one of the biggest gatherings of women and non-binary technologists, the Grace Hopper Celebration. “Unlike past events, this year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below our expectations and, ultimately, below the level needed to cover critical operating expenses,” the organizers wrote in a statement. Bloomberg reported that this comes after years of declining attendance, with around 15,000 people attending in 2025, making it the fewest since 2016.

In 2023, GHC attendees reported standing in lines for hours to talk to recruiters, being shoved, harassed, and cut in front of by the hundreds of men who’d suddenly flooded the conference. “They trampled over attendees, shoved their way into the recruiter’s booth to wave their resumes in front of their faces, verbally assaulted attendees, and physically pushed and shoved attendees in line,” one attendee said.

After the GHC 2026 cancellation was announced, Kayley Seow, a tech worker who was at the 2023 conference, contacted me to talk about what it meant to her. She said she felt “pretty shattered” when she heard the conference wouldn’t happen this year. “GHC is such a pillar of the community that you don't expect to fall, or in this case, not run. Despite its flaws, it continues to be an important space for people hoping to get into tech and those already in it. I'd been recommending it to every undergrad or woman technologist to attend.” There are other, similar conferences held around the country, but GHC is hard to recreate, Seow told me. “Other organizations exist but they operate virtually, there's events here and there in the Bay, but it's impossible to find something as concentrated as GHC.”

The people she knows who are most affected are current undergrads who planned to go to GHC to connect with recruiters, find internships, and land graduate jobs, Seow said. “They're disappointed, and a little scared, since it's October and we're coming up on the end of internship recruiting season, especially for the international students who were hoping to talk to the bigger companies at GHC that have the resources to take on international students as interns.” It’s still unclear whether there will be a conference in 2027.

GHC’s cancellation this year follows a string of blows to organizations that support women technologists. Women Who Code, a nonprofit that awarded more than $3.5 million in scholarships and supported a community of 360,000 members, shut down in 2024 after 11 years, citing funding issues.

Things are very different today than they were when Mayer was the first-ever pregnant CEO of a Fortune 500 company. In 2025, at the direction of President Donald Trump’s executive order “Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferencing” and other orders, civil servants across the federal government from NASA to the Social Security office and the CDC had to drop everything to scrub mentions of diversity, equity and inclusion from their systems. This wasn’t just symbolic or semantic. The National Institutes of Health terminated billions of dollars worth of nearly 2,300 federal research grants, cuts that disproportionately affected women and early career researchers. Led entirely by inexperienced men in their early 20s and spearheaded by Elon Musk, the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency canceled funding that would have advanced potentially lifesaving research projects focused on pregnancy and reproductive health, chronic illness, and vaccine safety for women. The damage done by DOGE cuts to the advancement of science and technology that would have been done by women and would have improved women’s lives around the world is immeasurable and widespread; it’s hard to imagine believing gender plays no role in STEM today in light of what we have seen under the Trump administration over the last year and a half, especially.

But in a way, Mayer is right: Drinking one’s own Kool-Aid is a non-gendered issue. Earlier this year, Sam Altman suggested AI generating podcasts to interact with your kids about their days and got similarly roasted for a week straight. He deserved it, and so does she.
40326fa4a2140ddc: BRASÍLIA, Oct 27 — Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva stunned the world with an election victory that has landed him an unprecedented fourth term in office.
Bets were on right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro to become Brazil’s next president after his shock first-round win earlier this month.
But the leftist incumbent bounced back with an energetic runoff campaign, going on to win 51.8 per cent of the vote.
How did 80-year-old Lula pull it off?
Young people take the streets
While the campaign reeled from the first-round defeat, students and young people immediately took to the streets.

Marching to slogans like “Bolsonaro never again,” thousands of people turned out in the cities of Rio de Janeiro, Sao Paulo and Belo Horizonte to rally support for Lula, his social policies and his promise to defend minority rights.
“The mobilisation of young people was fundamental,” said Eduardo Grin, a political scientist at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV).
Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT) “managed to reconnect with that young audience,” he told AFP.
The president himself said he had not seen anything like it since 1984, when a mass movement called for elections during Brazil’s military dictatorship.
Digital troops
Lula called his first-round campaign the most “disorganized” in decades and overhauled his social media strategy ahead of Sunday’s vote.
The incumbent sought help from young influencer politicians, bought his first cellphone and declared himself “king of the selfie.”
His supporters meanwhile launched a digital offensive of their own to counter the strong online influence of the political right.
Many leftists “spent hours and hours per day online just posting stuff or taking to the streets and talking to voters,” Oliver Stuenkel of the FGV told AFP.
“The social network activity was exhausting; I devoted a lot of time outside my working hours with the awareness that I was working for Lula,” publicist Taiza Mendonca, 36, told AFP in Rio.
Even Mendonca’s “60-year-old aunties” learned the word “hashtag,” she added.
The digital campaign spread wings via the “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel, which went from having 60,000 followers to almost 11 million in three weeks.
Rejection of rival
According to Grin, “the mobilization in the streets and on social media managed to create fear of a return of the Bolsonaro family to power and concern for democracy and social rights.”
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, was chosen to lead the political right by his father, ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his own loss to Lula in 2022.

His critics remember his administration for rising hunger rates, a poor handling of the Covid-19 pandemic, increased violence against minorities and environmental policies rooted in denial of climate change.
Bearing a strong physical resemblance to his father, Flavio called Jair his “compass” during the campaign, vowing to liberate him if elected.
Crowd pleasers
Lula passed a raft of crowd-pleasing measures in the run-up to the election.
Congress handed him a key victory by approving a reform that guarantees workers two days of rest per week, a cornerstone campaign pledge.

The government rescheduled October welfare payments to land before the runoff instead of after, along with a wave of debt forgiveness for small-scale entrepreneurs and a raft of other popular measures.
“I’m not going to stop granting a benefit I can grant just because there are elections,” Lula said in an interview on the campaign trail. — AFP
b1a3d64341f6e131: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 27 — As the world grapples with various uncertainties, food security has increasingly become a key concern.

Today, the issue is no longer merely about ensuring an adequate food supply, but also about a country’s ability to build a robust and resilient food system that can guarantee a consistent supply of quality food.

For Malaysia, strengthening food security requires a more comprehensive approach that goes beyond increasing agricultural and livestock production. It also involves transforming local produce into high-value food products through research and development (R&D), technological innovation and commercial-scale manufacturing capabilities.
One local company demonstrating such potential is Pure Mylk, a plant-based beverage contract manufacturer based in Pulau Indah, Selangor.
A contract manufacturer produces goods on behalf of other companies or brands.

Pure Mylk operates as Malaysia’s first contract manufacturer specialising in plant-based beverages, producing hundreds of product variations for various private-label brands in the domestic and regional markets.
Technology adds value to local products
Pure Mylk chief executive officer Marcus Khoo said the company was a pioneer in plant-based beverage manufacturing in Malaysia, leveraging biotechnology and food science.
He said that, unlike conventional beverage manufacturers, Pure Mylk offered end-to-end solutions encompassing research and development, product formulation, packaging and commercial production.

“Pure Mylk helps transform agricultural ingredients into food and beverage products that are safe, nutritious, commercially scalable and market-ready. Its services also cover research and development, product formulation, pilot testing, aseptic processing, packaging and large-scale production.

“The company produces a wide range of plant-based beverages, including oat, rice, almond, coconut, pistachio and walnut milk. Our strength lies not merely in producing the final product, but also in the technology we use to ensure consistent quality, safety and compliance with commercial manufacturing and market requirements,” he told Bernama.
Marcus said the key technologies employed by the company included enzymatic processing and the VTIS Direct Steam Injection ultra-high-temperature (UHT) aseptic system.

He said that compared with conventional systems, the technology was more effective in preserving the taste, colour, texture and nutritional value of products, while ensuring high food safety standards and a longer shelf life.
“The technology also enables products to be distributed over wider areas, reduces dependence on cold-chain logistics, minimises the risk of food spoilage and improves access to nutritious food.

“In the context of food security, this capability is particularly important because nutritious products can only deliver their full benefits when they are distributed efficiently and reach consumers safely, with their quality preserved,” he said.

Elaborating further, Marcus said Pure Mylk also offered contract manufacturing, private-label development, product development, and research and innovation support to local companies, including small and medium enterprises (SMEs), seeking to enter Malaysia’s plant-based beverage industry.
He said these services enabled companies to develop and commercialise their products more effectively through technical guidance and Pure Mylk’s technological expertise.

“Pure Mylk is committed to strengthening local innovation and manufacturing capabilities, which have traditionally relied heavily on imported resources, thereby reducing dependence on overseas supply chains.

“We see this effort as contributing not only to national food security but also to creating a collaborative platform that brings together local brands, start-ups and global technology partners to accelerate innovation and shape the future of Malaysia’s plant-based beverage industry,” he added.
Strengthening the national bioeconomy
Marcus said Pure Mylk also contributed to strengthening the country’s bioeconomy ecosystem by enhancing local manufacturing capabilities and improving readiness for halal exports.
He said the initiative aligned with the company’s objective of transforming agricultural raw materials into beverages with commercial potential in both domestic and international markets.

He added that countries seeking to establish control over their food systems could not rely solely on crop production, but also needed to master processing technologies, nutritional science and large-scale manufacturing infrastructure.

“Local food technology innovation now plays an important role in strengthening the national bioeconomy, while reducing dependence on imported finished products, foreign technologies and overseas expertise.

“By developing stronger local processing capabilities, Malaysia has the potential to move beyond being merely a supplier of raw materials to becoming a producer of high-value food products driven by innovation and technology,” he said.

As a BioNexus-status company under the Malaysian Bioeconomy Development Corporation (Bioeconomy Corporation), Pure Mylk also supports the regional agenda for sustainability, food security and the development of high-tech manufacturing industries across ASEAN, he said.

“For Pure Mylk, recognition as a BioNexus company reinforces its position as an innovation-driven food technology company and strengthens the confidence of investors, industry players, universities, government agencies and international partners in the company.

“Internationally, Pure Mylk is also involved in various industry-related projects and collaborations with industry partners from the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia and Japan, reflecting growing confidence in Malaysia’s food and beverage technology capabilities on the global stage,” he added.

Apart from its BioNexus recognition, another achievement by Pure Mylk is the development of a high-tech beverage manufacturing platform in Malaysia that meets international food safety and quality standards, including Halal certification, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) and Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP).
Ensuring food security
Marcus said food security should not be viewed solely in terms of food production, but must encompass the entire food supply chain.

He said the issue extended beyond ensuring sufficient food supplies to include how nutrients were processed, preserved, distributed, stored and made accessible to the public at affordable prices through large-scale production.

By mastering food processing technologies and strengthening local manufacturing capabilities, Malaysia could build a more resilient food system, reduce dependence on external supply chains and become better prepared for future food crises, he said.
Through the application of food science and processing technologies, agricultural materials that have been underutilised could also be upgraded to produce high-quality, value-added food products.

“For example, broken brown rice, often regarded as a low-value by-product of the agricultural supply chain, can be processed using enzymatic technology, milling and aseptic UHT systems to produce nutritious brown rice beverages with a smoother texture and longer shelf life.
“This approach not only optimises the use of agricultural resources but also helps reduce food waste and provides consumers with more accessible nutritional options,” he said.

Marcus said the company believed the future of Malaysia’s food industry depended on its ability to integrate science, biotechnology, manufacturing capabilities and food product commercialisation strategies into a comprehensive and integrated ecosystem.

In this regard, Pure Mylk aims to help position Malaysia as a regional hub for advanced food technology, large-scale nutritional innovation, and the development and manufacture of high-value beverages.

“Pure Mylk believes that the ‘Made in Malaysia’ label should represent more than products manufactured in the country. It should also reflect trusted quality, high food safety standards, halal excellence, science-based innovation and the ability of local products to compete internationally,” he said.
Bioeconomy Corporation extends support

Meanwhile, Bioeconomy Corporation chief executive officer Mohd Khairul Fidzal Abdul Razak said the corporation would continue strengthening its role in supporting local companies to drive innovation and enhance the country’s food supply chain.
He said supporting local bio-based companies was crucial to ensuring that innovations in the food sector could be developed, commercialised and expanded into global markets more effectively.
“Local innovation plays an important role in enhancing the capabilities of the food industry, thereby strengthening national food security.
“Our support for this company demonstrates that bio-based technologies have the potential to produce high-value-added products while developing more sustainable and resilient supply chains,” he said.

He said Bioeconomy Corporation also focused on developing an ecosystem that connected local companies with mentoring opportunities, industry networks, market exposure and more structured pathways to commercialisation.

The initiative was in line with the aspirations of the National Biotechnology Policy 2.0 under the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation (MOSTI), particularly in driving bio-innovation, strengthening sustainability and safeguarding national food security, he said.
“Amid an increasingly challenging food security landscape, food production capabilities alone are no longer sufficient.
“They must be supported by advanced processing technologies, research and development (R&D), manufacturing capabilities, and more efficient and sustainable distribution systems,” he said. — Bernama
a68c4238f4f26d05: TOKYO, Oct 27 — Tetsuya Chiba, a titan of Japanese manga best known for the legendary boxing series “Ashita no Joe”, has died aged 87, his publishers said Tuesday.

Chiba’s works often told stories about the physical and mental growth of young athletes across various sports including golf, boxing and the martial art kendo, while also showing the poverty, despair, joy and optimism of ordinary life in postwar Japan.

“Ashita no Joe”, published in the 1960s through the 1970s, featured a troubled young man who learns boxing in a juvenile detention centre and rises through the professional ranks to engage in epic rivalries.
The series became a cultural phenomenon.

Fans held a funeral after Joe’s main rival died in the story. Older fans can casually recite lines from the work, which also spawned enormously popular anime series, movies, video games, television commercials and theatrical productions.

Chiba, with a seven-decade career, also taught at university level, led the Japan Cartoonists Association, and received a number of Japanese cultural accolades, including the enormously prestigious Order of Culture, given to people who have made a significant contribution to art, science and culture.
Major publisher Kodansha has honoured his legacy with the “Tetsuya Chiba Award” for young manga artists for the past 46 years.

“Countless rookie manga artists took master Chiba’s words to heart as they embarked on the path to becoming professionals, and many of them are still active today,” the firm said in a statement, adding that he died last Thursday.
“Master Chiba’s tremendous contributions to the world of manga are truly irreplaceable.”
Another publisher Shogakukan credited him with helping to shape Japan’s manga culture and capturing the hearts of generations of fans.
“For seventy years, master Tetsuya Chiba has been at the forefront of the manga world. He created countless masterpieces,” it said.
Chiba also often gave media interviews to talk about his commitment to peace and discussed memories of his childhood in China during World War II before returning to Japan after its defeat. — AFP
5154072c97ec831a: LIBREVILLE (Gabon), Oct 27 — Each year, Gabon’s lush rainforests yield the discovery of previously unknown plant species to botanists like Archange Boupoya — who believes that this exceptional yet largely mysterious natural wealth needs cataloguing to save.

“We cannot preserve that which we do not understand,” said Boupoya, the director of the Sibang botanical garden, a sliver of tropical forest in the heart of the capital Libreville, brimming with orchids snaking up metal columns or floating down from the shaded canopy.
“So we’re continuing still today to identify this biodiversity so that we can save it.”

Together with a thirty-some-strong team of fellow botanists, Boupoya strives to make Sibang a sort of “museum of plants” for his central African country, 88 percent of which is still covered in jungle.

Understanding and protecting rare and exceptional species — a key theme of the United Nations’ COP17 conference on biodiversity which opened on Monday in Armenia — is both their life’s work and a monumental task.
“Unlike countries that are well-known botanically, like in Europe and Asia, Gabon remains very little understood,” he explained — despite the importance of the country’s forests for the whole planet.
Ten new species a year
For Gabon is part of the Congo Basin, considered the Earth’s second “green lung” after the Amazon rainforest, and a key natural sponge for absorbing planet-warming CO2.
Swathes of the country are carpeted with impassable jungles, with roads lacking.
“Each year, while conducting botanical surveys, we discover an average of 10 new species,” said Boupoya.
According to the director, botanists believe that the country is home to between 7,000 and 10,000 known plant species, of which around one-tenth are under threat.

As part of a four-decade partnership with scientists from the Missouri Botanical Garden in the United States, teams from Sibang “will go into the forest for two or three weeks, collecting plants before oven-drying them”, Boupoya explained.
After being meticulously documented in Gabon, botanists from the United States, Britain, France and Belgium are drafted into the work of identifying the samples.
For those as-yet unidentified species, the researchers have to offer a full description before having their discovery recognised by the international scientific community.
‘Guarantee their survival’

A few kilometres from the botanical garden, the 100,000 or so plants that make up the institution’s collection — whose oldest sample dates back to 1880 — are stored in alphabetical order in imposing metal cabinets at the headquarters of the national parks agency.

This precious archive of Gabon’s flora was transferred here after having escaped the fire that ravaged the collection’s former site, at the entrance of the botanical garden, in the middle of the country’s post-election violence of 2016.
The cabinets house a record of a biodiversity under threat, especially from creeping urbanisation, industrialisation, deforestation, mining and the fossil fuel-rich country’s oil industry.
“We’ve plants here that we’re trying to preserve to guarantee their survival,” Boupoya said as he passed a series of aquatic plant specimens pickled in alcohol for posterity.
‘Much to explore’
One such family of aquatic plants, the Podostemaceae, which resemble mosses and grow near waterfalls, are among the species threatened. Some of them have only been discovered recently.
But one of their habitats is threatened with destruction by the Kinguele hydroelectric dam, around 100 kilometres from the capital, whose construction is set to be completed within weeks.
Boupoya said he hopes that international donors could help relocate rare species which find themselves endangered by major infrastructure projects like the dam.
For their part, the botanists point to their increasingly tough working conditions.

Top among the list of complaints are inadequate facilities for plant conservation since the fire, a lack of funding and the pressure of urban encroachment on the Sibang botanical garden, whose surface area is shrinking year-by-year.

To help preserve Gabon’s dizzying array of plant life for the future, the botanists hope to benefit from private financing, notably through the sort of biodiversity credits dreamed up at a previous UN COP conference on protecting nature.
“We’ve still got much to do and much to explore,” Boupoya said, as he pointed to a map of Gabon showing the sheer size of the area of the country that remains undiscovered. — AFP
ebf0332be7a3381f: Nobody sets out to build file infrastructure that makes employees less productive. Yet sensible technology decisions made years ago can leave organizations wrestling with systems that no longer suit how their teams work.

Take network-attached storage (NAS). It has long provided a dependable way to store and access files. But what happens when the people using those files are no longer sitting in the same building, or even the same country?

A project team can spend its morning waiting for a multi-gigabyte file to transfer over a VPN, then lose more time checking whether the copy they received is the latest. No single delay attracts much attention. Repeat that across projects and the cost starts to add up.
The price of working around the problem
When shared access becomes difficult, employees find workarounds. They download local copies, duplicate folders, and transfer files between systems to keep projects moving.

Now imagine an architecture firm sharing a large building model between design offices. One team updates its copy while another works from yesterday’s export. Before anyone can move forward, someone has to reconcile the differences. That's time spent managing files rather than designing the building.
Duplicated data consumes storage capacity and complicates oversight. Meanwhile, IT must keep legacy infrastructure running while addressing performance, cost, security, and governance requirements.

Replacing every storage system is rarely a practical first move. Organizations have invested in infrastructure, access controls, and established processes. The sharper question is whether the way people access and collaborate on files needs to change.

The right starting point depends on which workflows create the most friction. Leaders need to identify the costs hidden in file transfers, local copies, and avoidable rework before choosing how to modernize.

Those are the issues The Register and LucidLink will put on the table at an invitation-only executive dinner in London on Tuesday, November 24. Moderated by The Register’s Joe Fay, the roundtable will examine modernizing file infrastructure while protecting existing storage and governance investments.
It's a chance to compare practical experience with peers who have faced the same uncomfortable question: when does a familiar system start holding the business back?
Request your place at the November 24 dinner
f9fa5fb43e63d1bb: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 27 — Malaysia may experience hotter and drier weather towards the end of the 2026/2027 North-east Monsoon (MTL), especially from late January to March next year, following expectations of a Super El Niño phenomenon that could lead to reduced rainfall across the country

Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) National Weather and Earthquake Operations Centre senior director Maqrun Fadzli Mohd Fahmi said these conditions could increase the risk of heatwaves and droughts, especially if rainfall decreases during that period.
He said the El Niño phenomenon is currently in a strong phase and is expected to intensify to a very strong level or Super El Niño towards the end of this year and into next year.

“With reduced rainfall, hot weather or heatwaves often emerge, along with drought due to water shortages caused by insufficient rainfall,” he said as a guest on Bernama TV’s “Fokus 15” programme today.

However, he said the initial phase of the 2026/2027 MTL, which begins today, is expected to bring three to five episodes of prolonged heavy rainfall, particularly between this November and January 2027.
He said that these conditions could heighten the risk of flooding, particularly in the East Coast states of Kelantan, Terengganu and Pahang, as well as eastern Johor.

“Residents in flood-prone areas should remain vigilant regarding the risk of heavy rain during the early part of the monsoon, while drier conditions towards the end of the monsoon will require preparations for possible hot weather and water shortages,” he said.

Maqrun Fadzli said MetMalaysia monitors weather developments around the clock and will issue heavy rain warnings when necessary to enable relevant agencies and the public to take appropriate precautionary measures.

He advised the public to always refer to latest weather information and warnings from official sources, make early preparations for possible floods and comply with instructions from the authorities, including evacuation orders when necessary.
He also reminded the public to avoid open burning during the dry weather to reduce the risk of localised haze. — Bernama

adcdc3890d6a4625: KANGAR, Oct 27 — A Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA) personnel was killed and three others injured when their boat collided with a concrete structure during an enforcement operation off Kuala Sungai Padang, Kuala Perlis, last night.

Kedah and Perlis Maritime director First Admiral Romli Mustafa said five MMEA personnel were conducting the operation at 11.37pm to intercept a boat suspected of carrying undocumented Myanmar migrants.

He said the suspected migrant boat sped towards the shore after being detected, triggering a 15-minute pursuit. The boat is believed to have rammed the MMEA vessel, causing it to collide with a concrete structure near the Malaysian Fisheries Development Authority (LKIM) jetty at Kuala Sungai Padang.

“The impact threw three of the five personnel overboard, including one who was reported missing. He was found floating in the sea at about 1.30am today, unconscious, and was pronounced dead. He was believed to have sustained serious head injuries,” he told a press conference here today.
Romli said the three injured personnel suffered a fractured wrist, chest pain, and pain on both sides of the ribs. All were taken to Hospital Tuanku Fauziah for further examination and treatment.
The deceased was taken to Sultanah Bahiyah Hospital in Alor Setar, Kedah, for a post-mortem. His remains are expected to be buried in his hometown at Kuala Nerang, Kedah, after Asar prayers.
The deceased was identified as Mohd Roshaimi Mohd Ridzuan, 41, an MMEA technical personnel.
Romli said nine suspected undocumented Myanmar migrants, comprising seven men and two women, and two Thai male boat operators were detained in the incident.
“Checks found that all those detained were suspected of offences under the Immigration Act 1959/63 and the Anti-Trafficking in Persons and Anti-Smuggling of Migrants Act 2007 (ATIPSOM).
“They have been taken to the Kuala Perlis Maritime Zone headquarters for further investigation,” he said.
Romli said the MMEA would investigate the incident to determine its exact cause, stressing that personnel safety remained a priority during enforcement operations.
He added that efforts to combat the entry of undocumented migrants through the country’s maritime routes would continue to be strengthened.
The MMEA also extended its condolences to the deceased’s family and expressed appreciation for his service in protecting the country’s waters. — Bernama

1baaa9dac0c9db1c: Last week, I mentioned the long, distasteful history of governments deliberately underreporting inflation data.
It drew surprising pushback — especially given the chronological list I shared:

1944-45: Mitchell Committee 1953: Postwar Basket Revisions. 1961: Stigler Committee 1972-75: Core Inflation 1983: Owners’ equivalent rent 1995–96: Boskin Commission 2017: Chained CPI as fiscal policy 2000: Fed changes its target to PCE 2004: Fed changes its target to Core PCE 2020–26: Annualizing 2025: Suspending CPI
Those are the major historical changes designed to underreport inflation; I tried — but failed — to find similar actions that overreported inflation.
Hence, I characterize the focus on Core as a deliberate attempt to mislead an audience.1

To those who waived off the hot October 14th CPI print of 3.7%, including Food & Energy, and chose to focus instead on the much milder Core of 2.6% — here is my Core CPI challenge: You may focus on Core inflation, so long as you limit your consumption to only the goods included in the Core PCE/CPI.

Until the November 10 CPI release, you must avoid consuming any headline goods (same for the recent 6.3% PPI versus 5% Core PPI). You only have to wait until November 13 to consume food, beverages, travel, heat, electricity, etc.

You can buy all the new and used cars and trucks you want, plus tires and replacement parts! Just no gas or diesel. Shop for Clothing, jewelry, watches, and shoes, too — walking is healthy! I can’t say I know how you’re gonna process the transaction without energy.

Computers, smartphones, televisions, audio equipment, and software; medical goods, prescriptions/over-the-counter drugs, recreational goods, toys, sporting equipment, musical instruments, books, pet products, textbooks, school supplies, shampoo, toothpaste, cosmetics, razors, and perfume. Buy home furnishings, mattresses, carpets, appliances, and household supplies. And Bicycles — you can carry your new mattress home on a bike! Just no E-Bikes.
Tap water! Fasting and exercise can be very healthy!
Do you smoke? Tobacco is in the core — so is Alcohol for when you get bored of tap water…

That is my Core CPI challenge for any pundit discussing inflation: Skip the full headline inflation reading to discuss inflation ex-food and energy, and you must exclude food and energy until the next print.
Below you will find a handy set of inflation report calendars to let you know when you can buy gas, use electricity, or eat again…
Previously: The Long History of Underreporting Inflation (October 19, 2026)
1. In the event of a sudden and unexpected weather calamity, of course, you can disregard that lone print. But I mean a major earthquake or a Hurricane Sandy — not “Gee, it got cold in February…”
1707507850bbf0ea: Microsoft has released another out-of-band update for Windows, but this one isn't an emergency fix for the latest breakages. This time, it's all about certificates.

The non-security out-of-band release applies to supported OSes ranging from Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025, to Windows 10. It's all about updating the current certificate trust list (CTL) of devices that cannot access Microsoft's certificate-update service, or where automatic CTL updates are disabled.
It also contains everything in the October 13 update, including the ongoing VPN issues and the change that could break on-premises Exchange Servers.
There might also be oddities with Smart App Control, audio, and Remote Desktop connections for non-admin users, all of which are known issues in the October 13 update.
These problems are not resolved in this patch, so be aware of this when installing it.

It is also worth remembering that many devices will not need this version since the current certificate list updates usually come down through the update service. However, if that service isn't available or being used, it might be a good idea to get this out-of-band fix (while keeping the known issues in mind), since problems can occur when verifying certificates used by applications or websites.

The OOB update came after Microsoft laid out its response to the compromised eMudhra certificate keys. The Indian certification authority's private keys were compromised earlier this month, requiring a massive cleanup effort. According to Microsoft, "they could potentially be used to create certificates or sign content that appeared to come from a trusted CA [certificate authority]."

Like many other organizations, Microsoft moved swiftly to block the affected certificate authorities. It did so by updating its Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List to block the affected certificates. There was also a separate CRLSet release for Edge and WebView2.

According to the Windows behemoth, "On October 26, Microsoft released an out-of-band Windows update that removes seven certificates associated with the affected hierarchies: six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign, from the Windows trust list."

Microsoft's out-of-band patches are usually released after the company breaks a product and needs to issue an emergency fix. This time, the revision is due to Somebody Else's Problem and a need to get a CTL update out to devices that are disconnected from CTL updates. ®
2741ff75f1cf06c9: PETALING JAYA: The recent sell-off of Oriental Kopi Holdings Bhd shares following boycott calls over its omission of the national language in its menus is unwarranted, said a research house.
Hong Leong Investment Bank (HLIB) also said calls to boycott its kopitiam outlets had so far not affected sales, with no significant change in outlet footfall.
“We remain constructive on Oriental Kopi, as our call with management suggests the recent boycott calls over its menu language have, thus far, not impacted sales,” it said in a note.
The controversy blew up in early October after a social media user complained about the absence of a Malay translation in its menus, which are in English and Chinese.
Its shares have dropped as much as 10% in the aftermath of the menu controversy. It closed at 82 sen today, valuing the group at RM1.64 billion.
Its shares, which have been on steady decline since February, have fallen 42% year to date due to a combination of earnings misses, margin compression, and high expansion costs.
The menu backlash prompted Oriental Kopi founder Calvin Chan to apologise and promise improvements.
The company has since completed the design of a new trilingual menu, with the reprinting cost estimated at RM150,000 for about 2,000 menu books.
HLIB considers the management's response to the controversy “proactive and constructive”.
The bank maintained its “buy” call on the stock with an unchanged target price of RM1.17 a share and views the recent share-price weakness as “an attractive entry opportunity”.
It also kept its earnings forecasts unchanged and expects FY2026 core net profit to touch RM67 million.
Known for egg tarts, coffee and local dishes served in the tradition of Chinese coffee shops, Oriental Kopi was listed on the Ace Market in January 2025.
Its share price nearly doubled on its debut to 87.5 sen from its IPO price of 44 sen.
Founded in Johor in 2020, the group operates more than 30 outlets in Malaysia and Singapore and is targeting the opening of about 10 outlets annually.

da0ae5c7944f9c4a: Ohio ranks No. 4 in the U.S. in terms of how many data centers it has, including this one in Springfield. Michael M. Santiago/Getty ImagesData centers require enormous investments: land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return. Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to growing opposition to their construction, from Ohio to Texas. That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of US$156 billion in proposed data center projects in 2025 alone. We are professors who study real estate and urban economics, including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built? To find out, we teamed up with four colleagues to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops. How data centers create local jobs Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them. First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment. Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores and other local services. Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier. Data centers, like this one run by Amazon Web Services in New Carlisle, Ind., employ few people. Noah Berger/Getty Images via Amazon Web Services Tracking data centers and jobs We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U.S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages and the number of businesses in each county. Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center. To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers – such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others – before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains. Jobs appear, but not immediately During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers. Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7.4 more nonconstruction local jobs. Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1.7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2.7 nonconstruction jobs per megawatt of eventual data center capacity. A large 100-megawatt facility, for example, would be correlated with roughly 275 additional local jobs outside the data center itself. The Stargate Oracle AI data center, which is under construction in Abilene, Texas, will span roughly 4 million square feet and will be operated by Oracle for OpenAI. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Jobs are not where you might expect The types of jobs created help explain what is happening. Employment gains are concentrated in transportation and warehousing, professional and technical services and real estate. These industries may serve or benefit directly from data centers or from the investment and infrastructure they bring. By contrast, we found little evidence of job growth in restaurants, stores and other local services. We also found that more data center investment tends to follow in the same county. Most often, the companies already operating in a county expand their facilities. Other companies generally don’t move into that same area to build new data centers. Jobs are only one side of the equation Our study has limits. It covers data centers that opened through 2023, before the current wave of massive facilities were built to power AI. Larger data centers do not necessarily create proportionally more jobs, so our findings may not apply to today’s biggest projects. We also looked only at job gains and did not explore whether data centers are worth their cost to local communities. These facilities consume large amounts of electricity and water, can generate noise and may receive substantial tax breaks from local and state governments. We did not address any of those concerns. Our findings do show that data centers can create jobs beyond the small number of people working inside their walls. But that does not mean every one of them is a good deal for their local community. And whether those additional jobs justify the costs remains an open question. Simon Buechler receives funding from the Real Estate Research Institute (RERI). Lyndsey Rolheiser receives funding from the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) and the Real Estate Research Institute (RERI).
0400309918d0eb88: An injured woman is helped by two neighbors following a Russian airstrike in Sloviansk, Ukraine, on Oct. 11, 2026. Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu via Getty ImagesVladimir Putin has a theory of victory in Ukraine. It’s not the Russian president’s first theory – that was a quick, dayslong campaign – nor his second or third, which involved different land offensives in the east that quickly petered out. Instead, Putin’s latest hypothesis is that the relentless bombing of Ukrainian cities will impose so much hardship on civilians that they will concede to Russia’s war aims. Yet, as experts on conflict and public opinion, we believe there is a significant problem with this idea. Chiefly, extensive academic research shows that airpower alone rarely achieves decisive political goals. Bombs terrorize civilians, but our survey findings in Ukraine suggest they don’t change war outcome preferences. Indeed, recent data shows that suffering from power outages and wartime stress in Ukraine has no relationship to support for territorial concessions to Putin. Putin’s plan for destruction The targeting of Ukraine infrastructure has been part of Russia’s way of war since the invasion of February 2022. But since August 2026, Russia has significantly stepped up its attacks against Ukrainian power plants and grid systems, especially in Kyiv. And due to Ukrainian air defense shortages, more of Moscow’s missiles and jet-powered drones are finding their targets. Russia aims to degrade the quality of life of Ukrainians, depriving them of electricity, water and transportation, according to a recently intercepted Russian military document. “Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, adding: “Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating.” Ukrainians wait for a bus during a power outage in Kyiv on Oct. 22, 2026. Yuliia Ovsiannikova/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images The broader Russian aim appears to be to make the Ukrainian capital uninhabitable, imposing so much hardship that residents will either depart or revolt against continued war. In combination with more aggressive Russian tactics and hard-right Ukraine skepticism in Europe, Putin calculates Ukraine will eventually be broken, isolated and defeated. The city destruction strategy is not a new method of warfare by the Russian state. Post-Soviet Russia first employed a version of it during the first Chechen war of the mid 1990s, when much of the city of Grozny was reduced to rubble. The strategy was later revived by Russian airplanes in Aleppo, Syria. But is there any evidence for Putin’s theory of victory? Polling suggests not. Along with the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, we polled a nationally representative sample of 1,801 Ukrainians from June 9-26, 2026. The survey used a computer-aided telephone questionnaire and the results shown were proportionately weighted to accurately portray the view of residents in the area controlled by the Ukrainian government in Kyiv. It was the latest in a series of such nationwide polls we have conducted since December 2019. Ukraine’s war trauma There is no question that the Ukrainian population has been deeply traumatized by the escalation of the war since 2022. We asked Ukrainians nine well-being questions, which enabled us to create a stress index computed from how often they have experienced psychological symptoms since February 2022. The results on the index reveal that nearly 1 in 4 Ukrainians suffer from high levels of stress characterized by concentration problems, depression, irritability, distrust, physical weakness and other physical problems. More than 40% of the respondents in the latest survey indicated that they experienced two indicators of stress – nervousness and anxiety – often or nearly always. Stress is also related to war exposures. Asked about experiences of violence, roughly 20% of respondents said that they or a family member were personally injured due to Russian attacks, and 20% have directly witnessed violence by Russian forces. Sixty-nine percent of Ukrainians have a family member or close friend who has died as a result of this war. Power outages have been rampant across the country over the past year, disrupting everyday life. Overall, 65% of Ukrainians reported losing utilities “often” or “very often.” Only 1.4% of Ukrainians report having never lost power since 2022, and just 9% say they rarely lost power. There are important regional differences, however. While 73% of residents in Kyiv report that they lost power “often” or “very often,” the corresponding figure for residents in the western region is 54%. The impact on war attitudes While levels of stress are highly correlated with experiences of violence and a frequent loss of utilities, we examined whether this cumulative hardship affects preferences for a ceasefire. The survey asked whether the current front line should be accepted as a ceasefire line for the sake of peace. The Ukrainian government has said it is willing to accept this position, but it remains controversial as it concedes part of the country’s territory to Russia, even if only temporarily. Zelenskyy announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that freezing the current line of fighting was an option for negotiating peace; the Russian government, for its part, still covets all of the Donbas region of Ukraine and more. Ukrainians are highly divided on accepting the current front line, with 39% of respondents in our latest survey indicating they would – with varying degrees of reluctance – be open to that possibility, compared to 38% who would not. Critically, experiencing violence first-hand appears not to shape Ukrainian willingness to tolerate the de facto partition of their country at the current front line. Further, neither those who are more stressed nor those who have experienced more frequent power outages are more likely to favor accepting the existing front line as a ceasefire line. Ukrainians not ready to concede Our polling data from summer 2026 is affirmed by more recent polling by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology that supports the argument that bombing will not make Ukrainians more accepting of conceding territory. In a survey fielded from Oct. 6-18, 61% of Ukrainians rejected giving Russia full control of the Donbas region in return for a ceasefire and security guarantees. Indeed, the institute has asked this question in seven polls throughout 2026, and opposition to conceding Donbas has risen from 54% in January to 61% over the course of the year. Kyiv has been pummeled by Russian missiles and drones in recent weeks. But among all Ukrainian regions surveyed, Kyiv respondents had the lowest support for conceding the Donbas territory. Another question from the October 2026 survey asked how long respondents are willing to endure war: 62% chose the option “as long as necessary,” a 14-point increase from April this year and the same percent as December 2025. The figure at the outset of the war in May 2022 was only 9 points higher. We know that historical evidence does not predict the future. Nevertheless, our survey results suggest that increasing wartime hardship against Ukrainians will not coerce them into accepting territorial concessions. There is currently no persuasive survey evidence that bombing Ukrainians will succeed in making them capitulate to Russian demands. Ukrainians are stressed, war-weary and hungry for peace – but not on Russia’s terms. dd5a3a9957255d2e: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Will the real Anthropic please stand up?

After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and how it believes it will change the world.

But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture, presenting it as different things to different people: an AI safety organization, a profit-driven megacorp, and a group hell-bent on creating superhuman technology.
These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? Take a new glimpse inside Anthropic.
—Will Douglas Heaven

How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping efficiently move power across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses.
The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.
Find out how solid-state transformers could help meet rising electricity demand.
—Casey Crownhart
Are we there yet? Exercise in a pill

We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks, without the workout.
The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.
Discover how close researchers are to developing an exercise pill.
—Cassandra Willyard

The problem with thinking you’re part Neanderthal
There’s a theory that many of us have an “inner Neanderthal.” The idea is that Homo sapiens and its cousin species once bred, leaving some people today with a trace of Neanderthal DNA.
This DNA is arguably the 21st century’s most celebrated discovery in human evolution. But in 2024, a pair of French geneticists called into question the theory’s very foundations.
They proposed that what scientists interpret as interbreeding could instead be explained by population structure—the way genes concentrate in smaller, isolated groups.
Find out what it all means for human evolution.
—Ben Crair
